question: Avery attacks with a [Guile] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron], and Nelson blocks with [Jerrard of the Closed Fist]. Does Avery shuffle?
answer:
Direct answer stands: yes, Avery shuffles Guile into their library — but that conclusion rests entirely on the card data and rulings you gave me, not on the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts.

Being plain about the citations: every numbered rule in the provided context concerns declaring attackers, banding/"bands with other" (508.1e, 702.22c–m, 802.3b), and redundancy of menace/shadow/melee/soulbond. None of those address face-down creatures, evasion like "can't be blocked except by three or more creatures," combat damage, or dies/put-into-graveyard triggers. So the numbered rules text I was given does not settle this question; I am not going to attach an unrelated rule number to it.

What the provided card data does settle:
- Turned face down by Ixidron, Guile is a 2/2 with no name, no text, no subtypes, and no mana cost [Ixidron ruling #4]. So it lacks "can't be blocked except by three or more creatures," and Nelson's single blocker Jerrard of the Closed Fist is a legal block.
- Jerrard of the Closed Fist is 6/5 and deals 6 damage to the 2/2 face-down Guile, destroying it; the 2/2 deals only 2 back, so Jerrard of the Closed Fist survives.
- Guile's third ability triggers when Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere and triggers from the graveyard itself, not as a leaves-the-battlefield ability [Guile ruling #0], [Guile ruling #5]. Losing the ability earlier (while face down on the battlefield) doesn't stop it; only lacking it while in the graveyard would [Guile ruling #7]. In the graveyard the card is Guile again, so it triggers and Avery shuffles it into their library.

Timing assumption: Guile was face down when combat damage was dealt. If it had been turned face up before blockers were declared, the single block by Jerrard of the Closed Fist would have been illegal.

Player count doesn't change any of this.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.
gold_text.603.10: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.6c: Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called “zone-change triggers.” Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but aren’t limited to, “When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .” or “Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .” (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone “from anywhere” is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.

answer_gold:
Yes. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. At that point, the Guile is face-up in the graveyard and has that ability.

(Guile's trigger does not fit the exception for "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers because it is a "from anywhere" trigger.)

question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
answer:
No. While The Scarab God is face down because of Ixidron, it is a 2/2 creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost, so it simply has no abilities — neither the upkeep drain/scry trigger nor the "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand" trigger exists to trigger [Ixidron ruling #4].

In the combat described, Archer's face-down The Scarab God (a 2/2) is blocked by Nia's Scathe Zombies (a 2/2). Each deals 2 damage to the other, so both are destroyed. Because the face-down permanent had no death-triggered ability at the time it left the battlefield, nothing triggers, and it does not come back to Archer's hand at the beginning of the next end step; it just stays in the graveyard (where it is again face up as The Scarab God card). Only a creature can attack or block, and only a player, planeswalker, or battle can be attacked, which the face-down 2/2 satisfies fine as an attacker [506.3].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as The Scarab God still being face down throughout the combat damage step. If instead it were somehow turned face up before it died (Ixidron leaving the battlefield does not by itself turn it face up, but another effect could), it would then have its printed abilities and its death trigger would work normally, returning it to Archer's hand at the beginning of the next end step [The Scarab God ruling #1].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents, though in a multiplayer game Archer would announce which opponent, planeswalker, or battle each attacker is attacking [508.1b].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.10a: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows: Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities, abilities that trigger when a player sacrifices a permanent, abilities that trigger when a card leaves a graveyard, and abilities that trigger when an object that all players can see is put into a hand or library. Two creatures are on the battlefield along with an artifact that has the ability “Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life.” Someone casts a spell that destroys all artifacts, creatures, and enchantments. The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures.

Any listed characteristics are the copiable values of that object’s characteristics. (See rule 613, “Interaction of Continuous Effects,” and rule 707, “Copying Objects.”)

cited_text.506.3: Only a creature can attack or block. Only a player, a planeswalker, or a battle can be attacked.
cited_text.508.1b: First, the active player declares attackers. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. To declare attackers, the active player follows the steps below, in order. If at any point during the declaration of attackers, the active player is unable to comply with any of the steps listed below, the declaration is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the declaration (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the defending player controls any planeswalkers, is the protector of any battles, or the game allows the active player to attack multiple other players, the active player announces which player, planeswalker, or battle each of the chosen creatures is attacking.

answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

question: Alaia casts [Biogenic Upgrade] targeting [Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11]. In total how many counters are be placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11?
answer:
Nine +1/+1 counters total are placed, leaving Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 with nine +1/+1 counters (assuming it had none before).

Step by step:

1. Biogenic Upgrade distributes three +1/+1 counters to its single target, Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's own static ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") is a replacement effect that applies to this event, so four counters are put on instead of three. Card text like this governs over the plain instruction on Biogenic Upgrade.
2. Biogenic Upgrade then doubles the number of +1/+1 counters on it. Per [Biogenic Upgrade ruling #2], doubling means putting a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the number it already has — that's four — and "other cards that interact with putting counters on it will interact with this effect accordingly." So Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect applies again: four plus one = five counters are put on.

Total counters put on: 4 + 5 = 9, ending at nine +1/+1 counters (so a 10/10 base 1/1 becomes 10/10).

Notes: if Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 already had counters, redo the doubling with that starting number and still add one extra to each placement. If you controlled a second copy, each would add one per placement ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #3]), and if multiple counter-modifying effects applied you'd choose their order ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #1], consistent with [616.1e]). None of this depends on player count, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.
gold_text.701.10e: Double To double the number of a kind of counters on a player or permanent, give that player or permanent as many of those counters as that player or permanent already has.

cited_text.616.1e: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen.

answer_gold: Nine. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability is a replacement effect that applies whenever counters are being placed on it When Biogenic Upgrade begins resolving, that replacement effect will add a counter, resulting in Alaia placing four +1/+1 counters. Afterwards, Biogenic Upgrade will then double the amount of counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. This results in an additional four counters being placed on it, which will then be modified by Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect again, resulting in nine +1/+1 counters in total.

question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?
answer:
Direct answer: Yes. Each storm copy of Elemental Eruption will also have Everdream spliced onto it, and Addison doesn't pay Everdream's {2}{U} splice cost again for the copies.

Important caveat about grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover mana symbols, mana pools, cost reduction, and characteristic layers — none of them address splice, storm, or copying casting choices. So this answer rests entirely on the authoritative card rulings supplied with the card data, not on the provided numbered rules:

- [Everdream ruling #4] — if a spell is copied, choices made while casting it are copied, so the copy has the same cards spliced onto it as the original. Splicing Everdream onto Elemental Eruption is exactly such a choice.
- [Everdream ruling #1] — the spliced effect happens last, so each copy first creates the 4/4 red Dragon Elemental token with flying and prowess, then draws a card.
- [Elemental Eruption ruling #2] — the storm copies are put directly onto the stack and are not cast, which is why no additional splice cost is paid and why they aren't counted by later storm spells.
- [Elemental Eruption ruling #0] — each copy must be countered individually; countering the original Elemental Eruption leaves the copies intact.

Count of copies: storm copies Elemental Eruption for each spell cast before it this turn. With only Ferocious Zheng cast beforehand, that's one copy (one extra token, one extra card drawn). This is player-count independent in principle — storm counts spells cast earlier in the turn regardless of who cast them, so at a multiplayer table there may simply be more copies, each still carrying Everdream.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.601.2b: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.
gold_text.702.47a: Splice Splice is a static ability that functions while a card is in your hand. “Splice onto [quality] [cost]” means “You may reveal this card from your hand as you cast a [quality] spell. If you do, that spell gains the text of this card’s rules text and you pay [cost] as an additional cost to cast that spell.” Paying a card’s splice cost follows the rules for paying additional costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h. Since the card with splice remains in the player’s hand, it can later be cast normally or spliced onto another spell. It can even be discarded to pay a “discard a card” cost of the spell it’s spliced onto.
gold_text.707.2: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, “{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.” Clone is a creature that reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.” After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can’t pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.

answer_gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.

question: Nova controls a [Torsten Von Ursus] enchanted by their [Felidar Umbra]. Allen activates the last ability of [Sorin, Lord of Innistrad], targeting the Torsten Von Ursus. What happens?
answer:
Honest answer: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not settle this. None of the provided rules (they cover collect evidence, blight, shuffling, craft, gift, manifest dread, permanent spell resolution, meld, and optional-cost "if you do" clauses) address destruction, replacement effects for destruction, umbra armor, Auras being attached, or returning cards from a graveyard to the battlefield.

What I can point to is the provided card data itself, which describes the interaction: Felidar Umbra grants umbra armor, "If enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura," and its rulings state that this applies whenever the enchanted creature would be destroyed, including by an effect that says "destroy" it, that it is mandatory, that it is not regeneration, and that the spell or ability doing the destroying is what causes the Aura to be destroyed. Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's last ability reads "Destroy up to three target creatures and/or other planeswalkers. Return each card put into a graveyard this way to the battlefield under your control." Read together, Nova's Torsten Von Ursus would not be destroyed (damage removed instead), Nova's Felidar Umbra would be destroyed instead, and because Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability is what put Felidar Umbra into the graveyard, Allen would return Felidar Umbra to the battlefield under Allen's control.

But I'm flagging answered=false as instructed, because that conclusion rests on the card text and rulings rather than on any of the numbered rules supplied to me. To ground it in the Comprehensive Rules I would need the rules on replacement effects (rule 614), destruction and lethal damage (rules 701.7 and 120.6), and Auras entering the battlefield and attachment (rule 303).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.303.4f: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura’s enchant ability and any other applicable effects.
gold_text.702.89a: Umbra Armor Umbra armor is a static ability that appears on some Auras. “Umbra armor” means “If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura.”

answer_gold: The Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead of the Torsten Von Ursus. It is then returned to the battlefield by the rest of Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability. The only creature on the battlefield is the Torsten Von Ursus, so the Felidar Umbra must enter the battlefield enchanting the Torsten Von Ursus. Felidar Umbra is now controlled by Allen.

question: Nico controls [Containment Priest]. Alma attempts to play [Dryad Arbor], which is exiled. Can Alma now play [Sequestered Stash] as their land for turn?
answer:
No — Alma cannot play Sequestered Stash this turn (absent an effect granting an extra land play).

I want to be transparent about grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover mana abilities, basic land types, and mana production (e.g. [305.6], [605.2], [106.5]) and say nothing about the one-land-per-turn limit or about replacement effects that exile a permanent as it enters. So this answer rests entirely on the provided card data and rulings, which do directly settle it:

- Dryad Arbor is played as a land: "It doesn't use the stack, it's not a spell, it can't be responded to, it has no mana cost, and it counts as your land play for the turn" [Dryad Arbor ruling #4]. That means the land play is consumed by the act of playing Dryad Arbor.
- Dryad Arbor is a nontoken Land Creature that was played, not cast, so Containment Priest's text "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead" applies and it goes to exile rather than the battlefield [Containment Priest ruling #1]. Containment Priest's printed text governs here over any general expectation that a played land simply enters.
- Nothing in Containment Priest or the rulings refunds the land play, so Sequestered Stash stays in Alma's hand.

This is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; Containment Priest affects creatures regardless of controller. If you want the exact rule text for the one-land-per-turn limit, that rule wasn't included in my context.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.116.2a: There are twelve special actions: Playing a land is a special action. To play a land, a player puts that land onto the battlefield from the zone it was in (usually that player’s hand). By default, a player can take this action only once during each of their turns. A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn. See rule 305, “Lands.”
gold_text.305.2: A player can normally play one land during their turn; however, continuous effects may increase this number.

cited_text.305.6: The basic land types are Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest. If an object uses the words “basic land type,” it’s referring to one of these subtypes. An object with the land card type and a basic land type has the intrinsic ability “{T}: Add [mana symbol],” even if the text box doesn’t actually contain that text or the object has no text box. For Plains, [mana symbol] is {W}; for Islands, {U}; for Swamps, {B}; for Mountains, {R}; and for Forests, {G}. See rule 107.4a. See also rule 605, “Mana Abilities.”

answer_gold: No. Regardless of what zone Dryad Arbor moved to, it was still played as Alma's land play, and Alma can only play one land each turn.

question: Norah controls [Blood Sun]. Ari plays [Dark Depths] and then destroys the Blood Sun with [Sultai Charm]. What happens?
answer:
Ari ends up sacrificing Dark Depths and getting the 20/20 Marit Lage token.

Step by step:

1. While Norah's Blood Sun is on the battlefield, all lands lose all abilities except mana abilities. Dark Depths' "enters with ten ice counters" ability modifies how it enters the battlefield, and per [Blood Sun ruling #5] Dark Depths loses that ability before it can apply. So Dark Depths enters the battlefield with zero ice counters on it. (Dark Depths has no mana ability at all, so nothing of it survives Blood Sun — see [Dark Depths ruling #0].)
2. Dark Depths' last ability, "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it...", is a state trigger ([Dark Depths ruling #1]). While Blood Sun is on the battlefield, Dark Depths doesn't have that ability (it isn't a mana ability), so nothing triggers, and its {3} ability is likewise gone ([Blood Sun ruling #3] — a mana ability is one that produces mana, not one that costs mana).
3. Ari casts Sultai Charm choosing "Destroy target artifact or enchantment" targeting Blood Sun. Once Blood Sun leaves the battlefield, its continuous ability stops applying and Dark Depths immediately has its printed abilities again.
4. Because Dark Depths is on the battlefield with no ice counters on it, the state trigger's condition is already true, so it triggers right away. When it resolves, Ari sacrifices Dark Depths and creates Marit Lage, a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible. Note counters are not characteristics ([109.3]), but the trigger keys off the counters, not off characteristics — the point is simply that no ice counters were ever placed.

One caveat: if Dark Depths somehow leaves the battlefield before that triggered ability resolves, Ari can't sacrifice it and no token is created ([Dark Depths ruling #2]).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dark Depths entered while Blood Sun was already on the battlefield, as stated. If instead Dark Depths had entered first and Blood Sun arrived later, Dark Depths would already have its ten ice counters, and losing its abilities would just mean Ari can't remove counters with the {3} ability while Blood Sun remains — no free Marit Lage.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count; it plays out the same in two-player and multiplayer games (only the choice of legal targets for Sultai Charm can differ).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.12: Some replacement effects modify how a permanent enters the battlefield. (See rules 614.1c–d.) Such effects may come from the permanent itself if they affect only that permanent (as opposed to a general subset of permanents that includes it). They may also come from other sources. To determine which replacement effects apply and how they apply, check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account replacement effects that have already modified how it enters the battlefield (see rule 616.1), continuous effects from the permanent’s own static abilities that would apply to it once it’s on the battlefield, and continuous effects that already exist and would apply to the permanent. Voice of All says “As this creature enters, choose a color” and “This creature has protection from the chosen color.” An effect creates a token that’s a copy of Voice of All. As that token is created, the token’s controller chooses a color for it. Yixlid Jailer says “Cards in graveyards lose all abilities.” Scarwood Treefolk says “This creature enters tapped.” A Scarwood Treefolk that’s put onto the battlefield from a graveyard enters the battlefield tapped. Orb of Dreams is an artifact that says “Permanents enter tapped.” It won’t affect itself, so Orb of Dreams enters the battlefield untapped.

cited_text.109.3: An object’s characteristics are name, mana cost, color, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, abilities, power, toughness, loyalty, defense, hand modifier, and life modifier. Objects can have some or all of these characteristics. Any other information about an object isn’t a characteristic. For example, characteristics don’t include whether a permanent is tapped, a spell’s target, an object’s owner or controller, what an Aura enchants, and so on.

answer_gold: Dark Depths entered the battlefield with no ice counters, since it didn't have the ability that would cause it to enter with them. When Blood Sun is destroyed, Dark Depths triggers since it has no ice counters on it and creates a Marit Lage token.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with the {1}: change creature type ability, plus its own "{2}: Discard a card").

Why Yixlid Jailer doesn't stop this:
- Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." That strips the functional abilities of the Mistform Skyreaver card while it sits in the graveyard, but it does not erase or rewrite that card's text.
- Volrath's Shapeshifter's own ability is what's doing the work here, and it functions from the battlefield, not from the graveyard, so Yixlid Jailer doesn't turn it off. That ability is a text-changing effect [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5]: it gives Volrath's Shapeshifter "the full text of that card," i.e. Mistform Skyreaver's name, mana cost {5}{U}{U}, color (blue), types (Creature — Illusion), abilities as printed (flying; {1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn), and power/toughness 6/6 [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1]. Because the copied text is applied to Volrath's Shapeshifter on the battlefield, the flying ability exists there, where Yixlid Jailer has no effect.
- Volrath's Shapeshifter also keeps the granted "{2}: Discard a card" ability in addition to the copied abilities [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1].

A useful parallel: Yixlid Jailer's own ruling notes that "enters the battlefield with" abilities are stripped in the graveyard but still apply once the card is actually on the battlefield, because what matters is having the ability where it functions [Yixlid Jailer ruling #3]. Same principle here — the flying text matters on the battlefield.

What Yixlid Jailer would change: any ability of Mistform Skyreaver that would need to function from the graveyard itself (a graveyard-activated ability like scavenge or embalm, or a graveyard trigger) is shut off [702.97a], [702.128a], [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4]. Mistform Skyreaver has no such abilities, so nothing is lost.

Also note this doesn't involve any "enters" event — changing forms doesn't trigger enters abilities [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #4]. None of this depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Autumn controls [Bridge from Below] and [Silvercoat Lion]. They cast [Hour of Revelation]. Do they create a Zombie token?
answer:
No — Autumn does not create a Zombie token.

Grounding from the provided rules: Bridge from Below's own text conditions both triggered abilities on "if this card is in your graveyard," and rule [113.6k] explains that abilities of non-instant/sorcery objects function only where they can — a trigger condition that can't trigger from the battlefield functions in the zones it can trigger from, which for Bridge from Below is the graveyard. Card text overrides any general expectation here: Bridge from Below only does anything from a graveyard, and while it is on the battlefield it has no effect [Bridge from Below ruling #1].

Applied to your situation: Hour of Revelation destroys all nonland permanents, so Bridge from Below and Silvercoat Lion are put into Autumn's graveyard simultaneously. Bridge from Below was not in Autumn's graveyard immediately before Silvercoat Lion died, so its first ability doesn't trigger at all, and even if it had triggered it would need to still be in the graveyard on resolution to make a token [Bridge from Below ruling #0]. Its second ability likewise cares only about which graveyard the dead creature went to, not who controlled it [Bridge from Below ruling #3].

Secondary points:
- Cost note: Hour of Revelation costs {3}{W}{W}{W}; with ten or more nonland permanents on the battlefield when the cost is determined, it costs {W}{W}{W} — only the {3} generic portion is reduced, never the three {W} symbols [Hour of Revelation ruling #0].
- Multiplayer: same result with two players or more. Opponents' creatures destroyed by Hour of Revelation go to their own graveyards, but Bridge from Below still wasn't in Autumn's graveyard beforehand, so nothing triggers [Bridge from Below ruling #0]. Had Bridge from Below already been in Autumn's graveyard, Autumn could order simultaneous triggers to create a token before exiling Bridge from Below [Bridge from Below ruling #2].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.603.10a: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows: Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities, abilities that trigger when a player sacrifices a permanent, abilities that trigger when a card leaves a graveyard, and abilities that trigger when an object that all players can see is put into a hand or library. Two creatures are on the battlefield along with an artifact that has the ability “Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life.” Someone casts a spell that destroys all artifacts, creatures, and enchantments. The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures.

cited_text.113.6k: Abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack. Abilities of all other objects usually function only while that object is on the battlefield. The exceptions are as follows: A trigger condition that can’t trigger from the battlefield functions in all zones it can trigger from. Other trigger conditions of the same triggered ability may function in different zones. Absolver Thrull has the ability “When this creature enters or the creature it haunts dies, destroy target enchantment.” The first trigger condition functions from the battlefield and the second trigger condition functions from the exile zone. (See rule 702.55, “Haunt.”)

answer_gold: No. Leaves-the-battlefield triggers care about the state of the game immediately before the event in question. Bridge from Below was on the battlefield at that time, and won't trigger.

question: Axl activates [Ring of Ma'rûf]'s ability in their upkeep. What happens in Axl's draw step if they don't own any cards outside the game?
answer:
Answer unchanged, but let me be explicit about the grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided in this conversation cover this question. Everything given is about phasing (702.26a–n, 703.4a–c, 502.1, 610.4a, 603.10b, 702.26d/f/i/j/m, 514.2), and none of it addresses draws, replacement effects, or cards from outside the game. So I am citing no rule numbers, because there are none in the provided text that I relied on.

What the answer does rest on is authoritative card data you gave me: Ring of Ma'rûf's own text and its ruling.

Direct answer: in Axl's draw step, the draw is replaced by Ring of Ma'rûf's effect, and because Axl owns no cards outside the game, nothing is put into their hand — Axl draws no card that turn. Ring of Ma'rûf reads "{5}, {T}, Exile this artifact: The next time you would draw a card this turn, instead put a card you own from outside the game into your hand," and the Ring of Ma'rûf ruling states that rather than simply putting a card into your hand, the ability replaces your next draw, and that if you wouldn't draw a card during the rest of the turn the ability won't have any effect. Since it is a replacement of the draw and there is no card available to fetch, Axl neither draws nor gains a card.

Timing assumption: "upkeep" is not a Magic step; I assume Axl activated Ring of Ma'rûf earlier in their own turn (the beginning phase) so the draw-step draw is the "next time you would draw a card this turn." If Ring of Ma'rûf were instead activated after that draw had already happened, the effect would wait for a later draw that turn, and per the Ring of Ma'rûf ruling it would simply do nothing if no further draw occurs.

Ring of Ma'rûf is exiled as part of paying its activation cost either way, so it's gone regardless of the outcome. This works identically at a two-player and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.400.11: An object is outside the game if it isn’t in any of the game’s zones. Outside the game is not a zone.
gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.

answer_gold: Axl is required to attempt to find a card from outside the game, if they fail to find one, then when the ability resolves they will put nothing into their hand. Since Ring of Ma'rûf sets up a replacement effect, Axl can't choose to ignore it.

question: Athena control [Krark, the Thumbless] and [Spark Double] copying it. They cast [Song of Totentanz], which triggers both Krark, the Thumbless. When the first trigger resolves they lose the flip and return Song of Totentanz to hand. What happens when the second trigger resolves?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: the second Krark, the Thumbless trigger still resolves and Athena still flips a coin. If she loses that flip, nothing is returned to hand — Song of Totentanz is already in her hand, so the card just stays where it is [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #4]. If she wins that flip, a copy of Song of Totentanz is created on the stack even though the original is no longer there [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #12], with the same value of X chosen when Song of Totentanz was cast [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #3].

Honest note on grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover this interaction at all — they are about restarting the game (Karn Liberated), starting-player/draw-step rules, and subgames. So I am not citing any CR rule number, because doing so would be invented. This answer rests entirely on the card rulings supplied in the context, which do address the situation directly:
- Spark Double entered as a copy of Krark, the Thumbless and is not legendary, so Athena controls two permanents with the ability [Spark Double ruling #6].
- Both triggers went on the stack in an order of Athena's choice and are unaffected by Song of Totentanz later leaving the stack [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #1].
- Returning Song of Totentanz to hand removed it from the stack and it won't resolve; that is not countering it [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #14].
- A copy created this way is not cast, so no "whenever you cast" abilities trigger from it [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #2].
- Only creatures Athena controls as the copy resolves, including the Rats it makes, gain haste [Song of Totentanz ruling #0].

Timing assumption: I assume the losing flip was the first trigger to resolve, as stated. Had the winning flip resolved first, the copy would resolve before the original, and the later losing trigger would then bounce Song of Totentanz [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #15]. Nothing here changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.101.3: Any part of an instruction that’s impossible to perform is ignored. (In many cases the card will specify consequences for this; if it doesn’t, there’s no effect.)
gold_text.608.2h: If the object that’s resolving is an instant spell, a sorcery spell, or an ability, its resolution may involve several steps. The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last. If an effect requires information from the game (such as the number of creatures on the battlefield), the answer is determined only once, when the effect is applied. If the effect requires information from a specific object, including the source of the ability itself, the effect uses the current information of that object if it’s in the public zone it was expected to be in; if it’s no longer in that zone, or if the effect has moved it from a public zone to a hidden zone, the effect uses the object’s last known information. See rule 113.7a. If an ability states that an object does something, it’s the object as it exists—or as it most recently existed—that does it, not the ability.

answer_gold: If Athena loses the flip, nothing happens. If Athena wins the flip, a copy of Song of Totentanz is created.

question: Alden cast [Ixidron]. Natalie controls a very cute [Tangled Florahedron]. What happens to it?
answer:
Direct answer: Natalie's Tangled Florahedron is turned face down as Ixidron enters, becoming a nameless 2/2 creature with no text, no subtypes, no expansion symbol, and no mana cost — so it loses "{T}: Add {G}" and can't make green mana. It also counts toward Ixidron's power and toughness, since Ixidron's power and toughness each equal the number of face-down creatures on the battlefield.

Honest sourcing note: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (they concern restarting the game, subgames, the command zone, companion, and replacement-effect ordering) do not address face-down permanents or Ixidron at all. So this answer rests entirely on Ixidron's own printed text ("As this creature enters, turn all other nontoken creatures face down. (They're 2/2 creatures.)") and its provided rulings, which are authoritative on their own.

Supporting points from the card data:
- Face-down creatures made by Ixidron are 2/2 with no name, no text, no subtypes, no expansion symbol, and no mana cost; those face-down values are the copiable ones [Ixidron ruling #4].
- The turning happens *as* Ixidron enters, so there is never a moment with Ixidron on the battlefield and Tangled Florahedron face up [Ixidron ruling #3].
- Natalie may look at her own face-down Tangled Florahedron at any time; opponents may not, but she must keep face-down permanents easily differentiated [Ixidron ruling #2].
- Tangled Florahedron // Tangled Vale is a modal double-faced card, so it can't be transformed; its Tangled Vale land face isn't available while it sits face down as a creature [Tangled Florahedron // Tangled Vale ruling #3].

Timing caveat: if Tangled Florahedron were entering the battlefield simultaneously with Ixidron, it would enter face up instead [Ixidron ruling #1]. And if Natalie had played the card as Tangled Vale (a land), it wouldn't be a creature and Ixidron would leave it alone. This is the same whether the game has two players or more, since Ixidron affects all other nontoken creatures.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.712.16: Melded permanents and other double-faced permanents can’t be turned face down. If a spell or ability tries to turn a double-faced permanent face down, nothing happens and that effect doesn’t change any of its characteristics or their copiable values.

answer_gold: Nothing. Tangled Florahedron cannot be turned face down.

question: Amani controls [Leyline of the Void] and casts [Hypnotic Cloud] to have Nicolas discard a card. Nicolas discards [Loxodon Smiter]. Does it end up on the battlefield or in exile?
answer:
Loxodon Smiter ends up on the battlefield under Nicolas's control. Nicolas discards it, and Loxodon Smiter's own text — "If a spell or ability an opponent controls causes you to discard this card, put it onto the battlefield instead of putting it into your graveyard" — applies, because Hypnotic Cloud is a spell Amani (an opponent of Nicolas) controls.

Why Leyline of the Void doesn't get it: Leyline of the Void only replaces the event of a card being put into an opponent's graveyard with exile. Once Loxodon Smiter's replacement effect redirects it to the battlefield, it is never put into Nicolas's graveyard, so there is no graveyard-bound event left for Leyline of the Void to replace. Both are replacement effects modifying the same event, and the choice of which to apply belongs to the player who would be affected — Nicolas, the card's owner — and he will naturally choose Loxodon Smiter's effect. (The specific rule governing that ordering choice, 616.1, wasn't included in the context provided to me, so I'm relying on the card texts themselves; note that a card's own text takes precedence over a general rule it conflicts with.)

Also note the discard still happened: per the Loxodon Smiter ruling, putting it onto the battlefield this way still counts as discarding a card, so "whenever you discard a card" triggers still work. Likewise, per the Leyline of the Void ruling on discards, abilities that check a discarded card function even when the card doesn't reach the graveyard.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the number of players. Hypnotic Cloud targets one player, and Leyline of the Void applies to every opponent of Amani, so at a table of three or more the result is the same for whichever opponent was targeted. Also, Amani targeting Nicolas with Hypnotic Cloud is a crime.

If instead Nicolas had discarded some other nontoken card, that card would be exiled rather than put into his graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.
gold_text.616.1: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4).

cited_text.Crime: Crime. Targeting an opponent, anything that opponent controls, and/or any cards in an opponent’s graveyard is a crime. See rule 700.13.
cited_text.700.13: Some cards refer to committing a crime. A player commits a crime as that player casts a spell, activates an ability, or puts a triggered ability on the stack and that spell or ability targets at least one opponent; at least one permanent, spell, or ability an opponent controls; and/or at least one card in an opponent’s graveyard.

answer_gold: Whichever Nicolas prefers. There are two replacement effects applying to Loxodon Smiter going to the graveyard. Nicolas is the controller of the affected object, so they choose where it ends up.

question: In a Commander game with 4 players, Ari casts [Kardur, Doomscourge]. Bode controls [Oxidda Finisher], and [Parhelion II], which is not a creature at the time Kardur, Doomscourge's enter the battlefield ability resolves. During Bode's next turn, can they attack Ari with Parhelion II? Can they have the Angel tokens created by Parhelion II attack Ari?
answer:
Honest correction: the Comprehensive Rules text I was given in this conversation does not cover this question at all. The provided numbered rules are about restarting a game (727.1, 727.2, 727.4, 727.5, 727.6, 104.6), subgames (729.2, 729.2a, 729.4a, 729.5, 729.5a), starting decks/sideboards (103.2a, 400.11a), shuffling (701.24c), and merged permanents (730.3a). None of them address declaring attackers, attack requirements and restrictions, Vehicles becoming creatures via crew, or tokens that are put onto the battlefield already attacking. So I cannot ground a rules-based answer on the numbered rules supplied, and I'm setting answered to false.

What I can say from the card text and rulings that were provided (not from the numbered rules):
- Kardur, Doomscourge's own text says that until Ari's next turn, creatures Ari's opponents control attack each combat if able and attack a player other than Ari if able, and that requirement extends to creatures that come under an opponent's control later [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #2]. If a creature could legally attack multiple players, its controller chooses [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #3]; only if it can't attack any player other than Ari must it attack Ari [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #0]. Bode is also not forced to pay a cost such as Crew 4 to make Parhelion II attack [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #4].
- Parhelion II's Angel tokens are created already attacking, Bode chooses whom each is attacking, and they are never declared as attacking creatures [Parhelion II ruling #0], [Parhelion II ruling #1].

To state confidently how those interact — in particular whether a Vehicle that becomes a creature after Kardur, Doomscourge's ability resolved is bound by the attack requirement at the declare attackers step, and whether a requirement that applies at declaration reaches creatures put onto the battlefield attacking — I would need the actual declare-attackers and requirements/restrictions rules (roughly the 506/508 series), which were not provided here. Likewise, no multiplayer attack rules (choosing a defending player among several opponents) were included, so I can't formally distinguish the 4-player case from a two-player case using the given text.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.508.4: If a creature is put onto the battlefield attacking, its controller chooses which defending player, planeswalker a defending player controls, or battle a defending player protects it’s attacking as it enters the battlefield (unless the effect that put it onto the battlefield specifies what it’s attacking). Similarly, if an effect states that a creature is attacking, its controller chooses which defending player, planeswalker a defending player controls, or battle a defending player protects it’s attacking (unless the effect has already specified). Such creatures are “attacking” but, for the purposes of trigger events and effects, they never “attacked.” They remain attacking creatures until they’re removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.
gold_text.611.2c: A continuous effect may be generated by the resolution of a spell or ability. If a continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability modifies the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects, the set of objects it affects is determined when that continuous effect begins. After that point, the set won’t change. (Note that this works differently than a continuous effect from a static ability.) A continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability that doesn’t modify the characteristics or change the controller of any objects modifies the rules of the game, so it can affect objects that weren’t affected when that continuous effect began. If a single continuous effect has parts that modify the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects and other parts that don’t, the set of objects each part applies to is determined independently. An effect that reads “All white creatures get +1/+1 until end of turn” gives the bonus to all permanents that are white creatures when the spell or ability resolves—even if they change color later—and doesn’t affect those that enter the battlefield or turn white afterward. An effect that reads “Prevent all damage creatures would deal this turn” doesn’t modify any object’s characteristics, so it’s modifying the rules of the game. That means the effect will apply even to damage from creatures that weren’t on the battlefield when the continuous effect began. It also affects damage from permanents that become creatures later in the turn.

answer_gold:
Bode cannot attack Ari with Parhelion II, but they can choose for the Angel tokens to attack Ari.

Kardur, Doomscourge's enters-the-battlefield ability sets up a rules change that causes any creatures Ari's opponents control to have to attack if able and to have to attack another player if able. Since this is a change in the rules of the game, it affects Parhelion II even if it is not a creature at the time the ability resolves.

The Angel tokens are created attacking, but are never declared as attackers. Because of this, Bode can choose Ari to be the defending player for the tokens.

question: Aislinn controls two [Bramblewood Paragon]s and casts [Thunder-Thrash Elder]. What is the maximum amount of counters Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Direct answer: 8 +1/+1 counters, if the two Bramblewood Paragons are the only other creatures Aislinn controls.

On your point about citations: none of the Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me (they cover The Ring tempts you 701.54a–e, restarting the game 727.4, Roles 303.7a/704.5y, the world rule 704.5k, protection 702.16m, phasing 702.26p, unpreventable damage 615.12a, and cleanup 514.2) bear on devour, +1/+1 counter replacement effects, or entering the battlefield. So I am not resting this answer on any provided CR rule number, and I won't manufacture one. The answer instead rests entirely on the card text and the authoritative rulings supplied in the card data:

- Devour 3 on Thunder-Thrash Elder: as it enters, sacrifice any number of creatures already on the battlefield; it enters with three times that many +1/+1 counters. It cannot devour itself or a creature entering simultaneously [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #0], and the choice is made during resolution [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #1]. Devouring both Bramblewood Paragons = 6 counters.
- Thunder-Thrash Elder is a Lizard Warrior, so each Bramblewood Paragon adds an additional +1/+1 counter, and multiple Bramblewood Paragons stack [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #1] [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #2]. That is +2.
- Total: 6 + 2 = 8.

Timing assumption: the devour sacrifice and the Bramblewood Paragon replacement effects are all applied as Thunder-Thrash Elder enters, so the two Bramblewood Paragons still supply their additional counters even though they are the creatures sacrificed. The precise replacement-effect ordering rules (CR 616) were not provided to me, so if you want that ordering verified, check those rules. If Aislinn had other creatures instead, she could keep both Bramblewood Paragons and get 3 counters per creature devoured plus 2 (e.g., 3 other creatures = 11).

This result does not change between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1c: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,” “As [this permanent] enters . . . ,” or “[This permanent] enters as . . . “ are replacement effects.

answer_gold: Eight. Both Bramblewood Paragon and Thunder-Thrash Elder have replacement effects that modify how Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield. While Thunder-Thrash Elder is entering the battlefield the game checks which replacement effects to apply, and sees that there are two Bramblewood Paragons that want to place an additional +1/+1 counter on Thunder-Thrash Elder as well as a Devour ability. If Aislinn chooses to devour the Bramblewood Paragons, they will place an additional six +1/+1 counters on Thunder-Thrash Elder.

question: Abel crews their [Adrestia]. Nathalie activates their [Mobilized District] causing it to become a creature. After that resolves, Nathalie casts [Mirrorweave] targeting their Mobilized District. What are Adrestia's characteristics after Mirrorweave resolves?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged): after Mirrorweave resolves, Abel's Adrestia becomes a copy of the printed card Mobilized District — a nonlegendary Land with no power/toughness, no islandwalk, no crew ability and no attack trigger, and it is not a creature at all. It has only "{T}: Add {C}" and "{4}: This land becomes a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance until end of turn. It's still a land. This ability costs {1} less to activate for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control."

Important transparency point about my grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me in this conversation cover copy effects, Vehicles/crew, or animated lands — the provided rules are about life gain/loss and exchange (119.3, 119.7–119.10, 701.12c), lifelink (702.15b–e), replacement effects and zone changes (400.6, 614.13c, 616.2), and blight (701.68b). So I am not resting this answer on any provided rule number. I am resting it entirely on the card data I was given, which is itself authoritative: Mirrorweave's text "Each other creature becomes a copy of target nonlegendary creature until end of turn," plus Mirrorweave ruling #0 (only printed values and other copy effects are copied) and especially Mirrorweave ruling #5, which states this exact case: targeting an animated Mutavault causes each other creature to become an unanimated Mutavault, because the "becomes a creature" effect isn't copied.

Applying that: Abel's crewed Adrestia is a creature when Mirrorweave resolves, so it is one of the "other creatures"; Nathalie's targeted Mobilized District is unaffected by the copy effect and stays a 3/3 Citizen land. Adrestia copies only printed Mobilized District, so it loses legendary status, its artifact/Vehicle types, islandwalk, crew, and the Assassin/draw trigger, and it is no longer a creature — it can't attack. question: Ari controls a [Lunarch Inquisitors] that exiled a [Jasmine Boreal] when it transformed. Nyla casts [Moonmist]. Does the Jasmine Boreal return to the battlefield?
answer:

The only grounding I have is the card's own ruling, which does speak to it directly: if Lunarch Inquisitors somehow transforms into Avacynian Missionaries, the exiled creature remains exiled, and it returns only if Avacynian Missionaries later leaves the battlefield [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #5]. Moonmist transforms all Humans, including non-Werewolf double-faced Humans [Moonmist ruling #1], so Lunarch Inquisitors would flip back — but on that ruling Jasmine Boreal would stay in exile. Note also that in a multiplayer game, if Lunarch Inquisitors's owner leaves the game, the exiled card returns to the battlefield [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #3].

What's missing from my context: the rules on transforming permanents (i.e., that a transformed permanent is the same object and hasn't left the battlefield) and the rules governing "exile until [this] leaves the battlefield" effects.

question: Addison controls [Carth the Lion] and [Bioessence Hydra]. Addison activates the [+1] ability of [Dovin, Architect of Law]. How many times does Bioessence Hydra trigger?
answer:
Bioessence Hydra triggers exactly once, and that single trigger puts two +1/+1 counters on Bioessence Hydra.

A note on grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given all concern the declare blockers step (509.1, 802.4, 805.10d, banding, protection, etc.) and none of them bear on loyalty abilities or counters. So I am resting this answer entirely on the printed card text and the provided card rulings, which are authoritative grounding on their own — not on any numbered rule.

- Carth the Lion's printed text says "Planeswalkers' loyalty abilities you activate cost an additional [+1] to activate," so Dovin, Architect of Law's [+1] ability instead costs [+2] to activate ([Carth the Lion ruling #3]).
- The total cost is calculated before any counters are added or removed, and the counters are placed in one single payment rather than one at a time ([Carth the Lion ruling #0]).
- Bioessence Hydra's printed text reads "Whenever one or more loyalty counters are put on planeswalkers you control, put that many +1/+1 counters on this creature." That is one trigger per counter-placement event, scaled by the number of counters ([Bioessence Hydra ruling #1] confirms such abilities trigger when a player puts counters on a permanent). Two loyalty counters arriving on Dovin, Architect of Law in one event therefore yield one Bioessence Hydra trigger for two +1/+1 counters.

If Addison controlled a second Carth the Lion, the increase would be cumulative to [+3] ([Carth the Lion ruling #1]) — still a single Bioessence Hydra trigger, for three +1/+1 counters. Nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

answer_gold: Once. If a planeswalker's ability has multiple costs to add or remove loyalty counters, those costs are combined into a single cost.

question: Nico casts [Assert Authority] targeting Ainsley's [Blightsteel Colossus]. What happens as Assert Authority resolves?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: Assert Authority counters Ainsley's Blightsteel Colossus spell and exiles it; it is not shuffled into Ainsley's library.

But I should be plain about the grounding. None of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover countering spells, replacement effects that change a card's destination zone, or exile — the provided excerpts are about drawing cards, collect evidence, connive, delve, blight, Commander draft, and doing "as much as possible" when something is impossible (609.3), and none of those settle this interaction. So my answer rests entirely on the two cards' own printed text, which is authoritative ground truth here:

- Assert Authority: "Counter target spell. If that spell is countered this way, exile it instead of putting it into its owner's graveyard." The Blightsteel Colossus spell goes from the stack to exile.
- Blightsteel Colossus: "If Blightsteel Colossus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Blightsteel Colossus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." This only applies to a move into a graveyard. Since Assert Authority already sends the countered spell to exile, no graveyard event ever occurs, so Blightsteel Colossus's ability does nothing and the card stays in exile. The graveyard and exile are separate zones.

Cost note: Assert Authority costs {5}{U}{U}, and affinity for artifacts reduces only the generic portion — one generic less per artifact Nico controls, never below {U}{U}, which must be paid with two blue mana.

This result is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

What the provided material does and doesn't cover: the discard-and-copy sequence comes straight from Chain of Plasma's own text ("Then that player or that permanent's controller may discard a card. If the player does, they may copy this spell and may choose a new target for that copy"), so Amani making that choice while Chain of Plasma is still resolving is grounded. However, the rules excerpts supplied here deal only with ordering of objects (graveyard/library order, piles, APNAP choice order, merged permanents) and contain nothing about state-based actions, losing the game at 0 life, or what happens to a spell controlled by a player who leaves the game. So I can't tell you from this context, without guessing, exactly when Amani loses for having 0 life relative to the copy resolving, or whether Amani's copy still resolves and damages Campbell after Amani has left the game. Those points are genuinely missing.

Timing note: I'm assuming Amani's discard/copy choice happens during Chain of Plasma's resolution, immediately after the 3 damage, as the card's wording indicates; nothing in the context lets a player act between the damage and that choice.

Player count: nothing here changes based on two players versus more, except that with more than two players Campbell is simply another player at the table who can be chosen as the copy's new target; the ordering rule for simultaneous choices (rule 101.4/101.4c, APNAP order) would only matter if multiple players had to choose at once, which isn't the case here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.117.5: Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event (see rule 704, “State-Based Actions”), then repeats this process until no state-based actions are performed. Then triggered abilities are put on the stack (see rule 603, “Handling Triggered Abilities”). These steps repeat in order until no further state-based actions are performed and no abilities trigger. When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end. Then, if that player controlled any objects on the stack not represented by cards, those objects cease to exist. Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game. If the player who left the game had priority at the time they left, priority passes to the next player in turn order who’s still in the game. If Alex leaves the game, so does Mind Control, and Assault Griffin reverts to Bianca’s control. Then that player shuffles their library,” targeting Bianca. Alex puts Serra Angel onto the battlefield from Bianca’s library. If Bianca leaves the game, Serra Angel also leaves the game. If, instead, Alex leaves the game, Serra Angel is exiled. Alex controls Genesis Chamber, which reads, “Whenever a nontoken creature enters, if Genesis Chamber is untapped, that creature’s controller creates a 1/1 colorless Myr artifact creature token.” If Alex leaves the game, all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under Alex’s control leave the game, and all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under any other player’s control remain in the game.

cited_text.101.4: If multiple players would make choices and/or take actions at the same time, the active player (the player whose turn it is) makes any choices required, then the next player in turn order (usually the player seated to the active player’s left) makes any choices required, followed by the remaining nonactive players in turn order. Then the actions happen simultaneously. This rule is often referred to as the “Active Player, Nonactive Player (APNAP) order” rule. A card reads “Each player sacrifices a creature.” First, the active player chooses a creature they control. Then each of the nonactive players, in turn order, chooses a creature they control. Then all creatures chosen this way are sacrificed simultaneously.
cited_text.101.4c: If multiple players would make choices and/or take actions at the same time, the active player (the player whose turn it is) makes any choices required, then the next player in turn order (usually the player seated to the active player’s left) makes any choices required, followed by the remaining nonactive players in turn order. Then the actions happen simultaneously. This rule is often referred to as the “Active Player, Nonactive Player (APNAP) order” rule. If a player would make more than one choice at the same time, the player makes the choices in the order specified. If no order is specified, the player chooses the order.

answer_gold: The copy is put onto the stack targeting Campbell. Then the original Chain of Plasma finishes resolving and state-based actions are checked. Amani loses the game, and the copy of Chain of Plasma is removed from the stack before it would resolve.

question: Aspen attacks with [Hammers of Moradin]. During the combat damage step, they use [Time Stop] to end the turn. What happens to the tokens created by myriad?
answer:
The myriad tokens stay on the battlefield permanently. Time Stop's "end the turn" effect removes all attackers and blockers from combat and then skips straight to the cleanup step, so the end of combat step never happens — and myriad's delayed trigger to "exile the tokens at end of combat" never gets a chance to trigger, so the token copies of Hammers of Moradin simply remain in play.

Details:
- Myriad on Hammers of Moradin creates tapped, attacking token copies attacking each opponent other than the defending player, and says "Exile the tokens at end of combat" — that's a delayed trigger keyed to the end of combat step [Hammers of Moradin].
- Time Stop ends the turn: spells and abilities on the stack are exiled, attacking and blocking creatures are removed from combat, state-based actions are checked with no player getting priority and no triggered abilities put onto the stack, and the current phase/step ends with the game jumping to the cleanup step [Time Stop ruling #3] [724.1c]. Because the combat phase is abandoned rather than proceeding to its end of combat step, the exile trigger never occurs.
- The tokens also lose their attacking status when combat ends, but nothing exiles or sacrifices them; they are ordinary permanents from then on.
- Note that if any abilities did trigger during this process they'd go on the stack during the cleanup step, giving players priority and a second cleanup step [Time Stop ruling #2] — but the end-of-combat exile isn't one of them, since that step never arrives.

Player count: this only comes up at a multiplayer table. With exactly two players, the defending player is your only opponent and myriad creates no tokens at all [Hammers of Moradin ruling #3], so there'd be nothing to exile. With three or more players, one token is created per non-defending opponent, and all of those survive.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Time Stop resolves during the combat damage step, before the end of combat step begins, as stated. If instead Time Stop were cast and resolved after the end of combat step had already begun and the exile trigger had already resolved, the tokens would already be in exile and would stay there.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.511.2: Abilities that trigger “at end of combat” trigger as the end of combat step begins. Effects that last “until end of combat” expire at the end of the combat phase.
gold_text.603.7b: An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time. A delayed triggered ability will contain “when,” “whenever,” or “at,” although that word won’t usually begin the ability. A delayed triggered ability will trigger only once—the next time its trigger event occurs—unless it has a stated duration, such as “this turn.” If its trigger event occurs more than once simultaneously and the ability doesn’t have a stated duration, the controller of the delayed triggered ability chooses which event causes the ability to trigger.
gold_text.702.116a: Myriad Myriad is a triggered ability that may also create a delayed triggered ability. “Myriad” means “Whenever this creature attacks, for each opponent other than defending player, you may create a token that’s a copy of this creature that’s tapped and attacking that player or a planeswalker they control. If one or more tokens are created this way, exile the tokens at end of combat.”

cited_text.724.1c: Some cards end the turn. When an effect ends the turn, follow these steps in order, as they differ from the normal process for resolving spells and abilities (see rule 608, “Resolving Spells and Abilities”). Check state-based actions. No player gets priority, and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack.

answer_gold: They remain on the battlefield, and will be exiled at the beginning of the next end of combat step. ([702.116a], [511.2], [603.7b])
