question: Aspen casts [Greater Good] sacrificing their [Bane Alley Blackguard] which is enchanted with [Mystic Subdual]. How many cards do they draw?
answer:
Honest correction: the numbered Comprehensive Rules text provided to me in this conversation does not settle this question. Everything I was given from the CR concerns copy effects and the copiable values of objects (707.2, 707.3, 707.4, 707.6, 707.9a, 707.9b, 707.11), name references (201.5a, 201.5b), permanent status (110.5c), linked abilities (607.5a), replacement-effect ordering (616.1f), layers (613.6), double-faced spells (712.13a), and preparation cards (722.3c). None of those address how many cards you draw from a power-based draw effect, how -X/-0 modifications combine with a creature's printed power, or what happens when a creature's power is negative.

What the provided card data and rulings do tell me: Greater Good's ability is "Sacrifice a creature: Draw cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power, then discard three cards," and you use the sacrificed creature's power as it last existed on the battlefield [Greater Good ruling #0]. Bane Alley Blackguard is printed as a 1/3, and Mystic Subdual makes the enchanted creature get -2/-0 and lose all abilities, so on the battlefield Bane Alley Blackguard's power was below zero. The discard is mandatory and happens in the same resolution with no chance for players to act in between [Greater Good ruling #2], and if Aspen has fewer than three cards in hand they discard their hand [Greater Good ruling #1].

The missing piece is the numbered rule stating that a negative power is treated as zero for purposes of drawing cards (i.e., that an instruction to draw a negative number of cards does nothing). That rule was not included in my context, so I won't assert it as grounded. If you can supply the rule on negative power/effects that use a creature's power as a number, I can give a fully cited answer.

Two side notes that are grounded in the card data: Greater Good is an enchantment, so its sacrifice effect is an activated ability of a Greater Good already on the battlefield, not something that happens while casting it. And the count depends on timing — the power used is Bane Alley Blackguard's power as it last existed on the battlefield [Greater Good ruling #0], so if Mystic Subdual were somehow gone before the sacrifice, the relevant power would have been its printed 1 instead.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.107.1b: The only numbers the Magic game uses are integers. Most of the time, the Magic game uses only positive numbers and zero. You can’t choose a negative number, deal negative damage, gain negative life, and so on. However, it’s possible for a game value, such as a creature’s power, to be less than zero. If a calculation or comparison needs to use a negative value, it does so. If a calculation that would determine the result of an effect yields a negative number, zero is used instead, unless that effect doubles, triples, or sets to a specific value a player’s life total or the power and/or toughness of a creature or creature card. If a 3/4 creature gets -5/-0, it’s a -2/4 creature. It doesn’t assign damage in combat. Its total power and toughness is 2. Giving it +3/+0 would raise its power to 1. Viridian Joiner is a 1/2 creature with the ability “{T}: Add an amount of {G} equal to this creature’s power.” An effect gives it -2/-0, then its ability is activated. The ability adds no mana to your mana pool. Chameleon Colossus is a 4/4 creature with the ability “{2}{G}{G}: This creature gets +X/+X until end of turn, where X is its power.” An effect gives it -6/-0, then its ability is activated. It remains a -2/4 creature. It doesn’t become -4/2.
gold_text.109.2: If a spell or ability uses a description of an object that includes a card type or subtype, but doesn’t refer to a specific zone or include the word “card,” “spell,” “source,” or “scheme,” it means a permanent of that card type or subtype on the battlefield.

answer_gold: None. Greater Good checks the power of the creature on the battlefield, not in the graveyard. If a player is instructed to draw a negative number of cards, they draw 0.

question: Ari controls [Mana Reflection] and [Looming Spires]. Nicole controls [Damping Sphere]. If Ari taps the Looming Spires for mana, how much mana is produced, and of what type(s)?
answer:
Honest correction: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules provided to me above address this question. Every rule I was given concerns drawing from an empty library, state-based actions and losing the game (121.3–121.6a, 704.5b, 704.7, 104.3c, etc.), ending the turn or combat phase, shuffling, and doing as much as possible (609.3). Nothing in that set covers mana abilities, replacement effects that modify mana production, or who chooses the order when two such effects apply. So I can't ground a rules-based answer, and I'm setting answered to false.

What I can say rests only on the card text and ruling supplied as card data, not on any provided numbered rule: Looming Spires' ability is a mana ability with {T} in its cost, so Ari is "tapping a permanent for mana" for Mana Reflection's purposes ([Mana Reflection ruling #3]). Mana Reflection would double the {R} to {R}{R}; Damping Sphere then says a land tapped for two or more mana "produces {C} instead of any other type and amount." [Damping Sphere ruling #2] says that when multiple replacement effects would modify the mana an ability produces, you choose one to apply and then re-check the others, and none may apply twice. Applying Mana Reflection then Damping Sphere yields a single {C} (colorless mana specifically, which cannot pay {R}). Trying Damping Sphere first, it isn't yet applicable (only one mana), so Mana Reflection makes {R}{R} and Damping Sphere then applies, again giving one {C}.

What's missing to make this verifiable from rules: the rules on mana abilities, on applying replacement effects to mana production, and on who chooses the order of applicable replacement effects. Also note Looming Spires enters tapped, so it can only be tapped for mana once untapped, and nothing here changes between two-player and multiplayer games as far as the card text shows.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.5: A replacement effect doesn’t invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event. A player controls two permanents, each with an ability that reads “If a creature you control would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage to that permanent or player instead.” A creature that normally deals 2 damage will deal 8 damage—not just 4, and not an infinite amount.

answer_gold: {C}. As the ability resolves, Mana Reflection replaces "Add {R}" with "Add {R}{R}". Damping Sphere then applies and replaces that with "Add {C}". Mana Reflection won't apply again.

question: Natasha and Nico are playing Two-Headed Giant, and each controls their own copy of [Bloodbond Vampire]. Ariel controls [Wall of Shards], and on their next upkeep they put the third age counter on it. Can Ariel have Natasha gain one life and Nico gain two? If so, how many triggered abilities of Bloodbond Vampire will be put on the stack?
answer:
Honest correction: the Comprehensive Rules text provided to me in this conversation does not settle this question. The numbered rules I was given cover layers and timestamps (613.x), flying/vigilance redundancy (702.9c, 702.20c), Equipment and Auras (301.5f, 604.4, 702.6d), replacement-effect ordering (616.1f), continuous effects (611.3a, 113.12), and fragmented loops (732.3). None of them address cumulative upkeep, choosing targets/recipients for a cost paid once per age counter, life-gain triggered abilities, or how Two-Headed Giant teammates' life gain is treated. So I cannot ground this answer in the numbered rules I was shown, and I won't invent citations.

What the provided card rulings do say, for what it's worth: Ariel may choose a different opponent for each age counter or the same opponent multiple times when paying Wall of Shards' cumulative upkeep [Wall of Shards ruling #0], and paying cumulative upkeep is all-or-nothing — with three age counters Ariel either makes all three "an opponent gains 1 life" payments or sacrifices Wall of Shards [Wall of Shards ruling #1]. Bloodbond Vampire triggers once per life-gaining event regardless of amount [Bloodbond Vampire ruling #0], and in Two-Headed Giant a teammate's life gain does not trigger your own Bloodbond Vampire [Bloodbond Vampire ruling #1]. Read together, those rulings point to: yes, Natasha 1 life and Nico 1 life twice, giving three Bloodbond Vampire triggers (one on Natasha's, two on Nico's). But that conclusion rests on the card rulings alone, not on any numbered rule I was provided.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.24a: Cumulative Upkeep Cumulative upkeep is a triggered ability that imposes an increasing cost on a permanent. “Cumulative upkeep [cost]” means “At the beginning of your upkeep, if this permanent is on the battlefield, put an age counter on this permanent. Then you may pay [cost] for each age counter on it. If you don’t, sacrifice it.” If [cost] has choices associated with it, each choice is made separately for each age counter, then either the entire set of costs is paid, or none of them is paid. Partial payments aren’t allowed. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep {W} or {U}” and two age counters on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, the creature’s controller puts an age counter on it and then may pay {W}{W}{W}, {W}{W}{U}, {W}{U}{U}, or {U}{U}{U} to keep the creature on the battlefield. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep—Sacrifice a creature” and one age counter on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, its controller can’t choose the same creature to sacrifice twice. Either two different creatures must be sacrificed, or the creature with cumulative upkeep must be sacrificed.
gold_text.810.9: Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually. The result is applied to the team’s shared life total. In a Two-Headed Giant game, a player casts Flame Rift, which reads, “Flame Rift deals 4 damage to each player.” Each team is dealt a total of 8 damage.

answer_gold: Paying Wall of Shards' cumulative upkeep involves the choice of an opponent. The choice for each age counter is made individually, then the whole cost is paid at once. This means Ariel can make the stated choice, and the result of this is Natasha gains one life and Nico gains two life. Because of this, each player's Bloodbond Vampire will trigger separately, causing two instances of the triggered ability to be put on the stack. Although the players share a life total, gaining life happens to each player individually.

question: Nataly controls [Urza's Saga] with 2 lore counters on it. Alex casts [Magus of the Moon]. What does Urza's Saga look like?
answer:
Urza's Saga becomes a Mountain with only "{T}: Add {R}" — it loses its Urza's Saga land type and all of its abilities, including the Saga's chapter abilities and the {T}: Add {C} / Construct-token abilities it had gained from chapters I and II — and because it's still a Saga enchantment with no chapter abilities, Nataly immediately sacrifices it as a state-based action.

Details:
- Magus of the Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Urza's Saga is a nonbasic land, so it loses its other land types and abilities and gains the type Mountain plus "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4].
- The abilities Urza's Saga gained from chapters I and II are abilities it has, so they're stripped too; it keeps them only for as long as nothing removes them [Urza's Saga ruling #5].
- Magus of the Moon doesn't change supertypes or names, and it doesn't strip the Saga enchantment subtype — only land types [Magus of the Moon ruling #1]. So it remains an enchantment Saga that no longer has chapter abilities, and "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed" [Urza's Saga ruling #1].
- The 2 lore counters stay on it while it's on the battlefield, but they no longer do anything since there are no chapter abilities; chapter III never resolves, so Nataly gets no artifact search.

Timing note: this all happens once Magus of the Moon actually resolves and is on the battlefield, not on casting. If Nataly wants value, she must use Urza's Saga's abilities (for instance the {2}, {T} Construct ability) while Magus of the Moon is still on the stack; abilities of a permanent like Magus of the Moon function only from the battlefield [113.6j]. This answer doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, everyone's included.

Similarly, when an effect sets one or more of an object’s subtypes, the new subtype(s) replaces any existing subtypes from the appropriate set (creature types, land types, artifact types, enchantment types, planeswalker types, or spell types). It keeps those abilities for as long as it's on the battlefield"), and no chapter abilities. Because it has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed". question: Niko controls [Metallurgeon] and [Ornithopter of Paradise]. Avery casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Ornithopter of Paradise with both. In response, Niko activates Metallurgeon's ability targeting Ornithopter of Paradise. What happens?
answer:
Honest answer: the rules excerpts provided here don't contain the regeneration rules, so I can't fully resolve this interaction on the given grounding.

What the provided material does establish:
- Metallurgeon's ability ("{W}, {T}: Regenerate target artifact") is a legal activated ability targeting Ornithopter of Paradise, since Ornithopter of Paradise is an artifact (an artifact creature). Metallurgeon's own card text is the authority here.
- Prismari Command was cast with two modes, both targeting Ornithopter of Paradise. Per [Prismari Command ruling #0], if at least one target is still legal as Prismari Command resolves, it resolves and does as much as it can; per [Prismari Command ruling #1], if all its targets are illegal on resolution it does nothing. Since Ornithopter of Paradise is still on the battlefield when Prismari Command resolves, both chosen modes will be carried out.

What's missing: the numbered rules for the keyword action "regenerate" (what the regeneration shield replaces, whether it removes marked damage, whether the permanent becomes tapped and is removed from combat, and how many shields one activation provides) are not in the context, and neither is the rule governing the order in which a modal spell's chosen modes are performed. Both are needed to say definitively whether Ornithopter of Paradise survives the combination of 2 damage (lethal for a 0/2) plus "destroy target artifact" with only one regeneration shield available.

If you can supply rule 701.15 (regenerate), 704 (state-based actions for lethal damage), and 700.2 (modal spells), I can give a definitive resolution. Nothing in the provided context is two-player-specific, so the number of players at the table doesn't change the above.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.117.2e: Other kinds of abilities and actions are automatically generated or performed by the game rules, or are performed by players without receiving priority. Resolving spells and abilities may instruct players to make choices or take actions, or may allow players to activate mana abilities. Even if a player is doing so, no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving. See rule 608, “Resolving Spells and Abilities.”
gold_text.117.5: Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event (see rule 704, “State-Based Actions”), then repeats this process until no state-based actions are performed. Then triggered abilities are put on the stack (see rule 603, “Handling Triggered Abilities”). These steps repeat in order until no further state-based actions are performed and no abilities trigger. Then the player who would have received priority does so.
gold_text.608.1: Each time all players pass in succession, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves. (See rule 609, “Effects.”)
gold_text.608.2c: If the object that’s resolving is an instant spell, a sorcery spell, or an ability, its resolution may involve several steps. The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last. The controller of the spell or ability follows its instructions in the order written. However, replacement effects may modify these actions. In some cases, later text on the card may modify the meaning of earlier text (for example, “Destroy target creature. It can’t be regenerated” or “Counter target spell. If that spell is countered this way, put it on top of its owner’s library instead of into its owner’s graveyard.”) Don’t just apply effects step by step without thinking in these cases—read the whole text and apply the rules of English to the text.
gold_text.614.8: Regeneration is a destruction-replacement effect. The word “instead” doesn’t appear on the card but is implicit in the definition of regeneration. “Regenerate [permanent]” means “The next time [permanent] would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. If it’s an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat.” Abilities that trigger from damage being dealt still trigger even if the permanent regenerates. See rule 701.19.
gold_text.701.19a: Regenerate If the effect of a resolving spell or ability regenerates a permanent, it creates a replacement effect that protects the permanent the next time it would be destroyed this turn. In this case, “Regenerate [permanent]” means “The next time [permanent] would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. If it’s an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat.”
gold_text.701.19b: Regenerate If the effect of a static ability regenerates a permanent, it replaces destruction with an alternate effect each time that permanent would be destroyed. In this case, “Regenerate [permanent]” means “Instead remove all damage marked on [permanent] and its controller taps it. If it’s an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat.”
gold_text.704.3: Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. If any state-based actions are performed as a result of a check, the check is repeated; otherwise all triggered abilities that are waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, then the check is repeated. Once no more state-based actions have been performed as the result of a check and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, the appropriate player gets priority. This process also occurs during the cleanup step (see rule 514), except that if no state-based actions are performed as the result of the step’s first check and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, then no player gets priority and the step ends.
gold_text.704.5: The state-based actions are as follows:
gold_text.704.5g: The state-based actions are as follows: If a creature has toughness greater than 0, it has damage marked on it, and the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed. Regeneration can replace this event.

answer_gold: Ornithopter of Paradise will end up tapped and have no damage marked on it. Metallurgeon's ability will resolve first, regenerating Ornithopter of Paradise. When Prismari Command resolves, the game carries out the instructions in the order written. First, Prismari Command deals 2 damage to Ornithopter of Paradise. The replacement effect generated by the regeneration ability will not apply yet, as even though Ornithopter of Paradise has been dealt lethal damage, it would only be destroyed when state-based actions are checked, and state-based actions are checked when a player would get priority. Next Prismari Command tries to destroy Ornithopter of Paradise and the replacement effect applies, replacing the destruction event with Ornithopter of Paradise being tapped and having all damaged marked on it removed. Lastly Prismari Command finishes resolving and leaves the stack and state-based actions are checked. Since Ornithopter of Paradise no longer has any damage marked on it, it will not be die.

question: Ahmed controls [Bronze Sable]. They cast [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Solemnity] onto the battlefield. Does Bronze Sable get a phylactery counter?
answer:
No — Bronze Sable does not get a phylactery counter, and Phylactery Lich must be sacrificed.

Grounding note first: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided in this conversation (601.3/601.3e/601.3f, 400.7h, 406.3a–b, 702.170d, 702.138a–b, 702.35c, 702.103d, 715.3d, 701.65a, 118.8c) speak to counters, simultaneous entry, or replacement effects — they all concern casting cards from exile, graveyards, or libraries. So I am not citing any numbered rule; my answer rests entirely on the card data and official card rulings supplied above, which do directly settle this interaction.

How it resolves:
- Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Solemnity onto the battlefield simultaneously [Genesis Wave ruling #5].
- Solemnity's printed text — "Players can't get counters" and "Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands" — is therefore already in effect when Phylactery Lich's "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control" tries to place the counter. Solemnity stops counters from being put on an artifact both as it enters and later [Solemnity ruling #8].
- Bronze Sable is an artifact already on the battlefield, not an object entering with counters, so the narrow exception in Solemnity ruling #6 (which only spares counters an object would enter the battlefield with alongside Solemnity) does not apply.
- With no permanent bearing a phylactery counter, Phylactery Lich's last ability — a state trigger — triggers immediately and Ahmed sacrifices Phylactery Lich [Phylactery Lich ruling #0, Phylactery Lich ruling #2]. If that trigger were countered while the condition still held, it would trigger again [Phylactery Lich ruling #2].
- Side note: even had Ahmed wanted to, he could not have chosen an artifact entering simultaneously with Phylactery Lich [Phylactery Lich ruling #1]; Bronze Sable was a legal choice only because it was already on the battlefield.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both Phylactery Lich and Solemnity arrive from the same Genesis Wave resolution, as described. The result is the same if Solemnity was already on the battlefield beforehand. Only if Solemnity were not yet on the battlefield when Phylactery Lich entered would Bronze Sable get the counter, and Solemnity entering later would not remove it [Solemnity ruling #0].

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.17a: Some effects state that something can’t happen. These effects aren’t replacement effects, but follow similar rules. “Can’t” effects must exist before the appropriate event occurs—they can’t “go back in time” and change something that’s already happened.

answer_gold: Yes. Phylactery Lich and Solemnity enter the battlefield at the same time. Solemnity's effect must exist before Phylactery Lich enters the battlefield in order to prevent Bronze Sable from getting a counter.

question: Ashley controls [Tatterkite]. Ashley casts [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Humility] onto the battlefield. Can they put a phylactery counter on Tatterkite?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given don't settle this question. Every numbered rule in my context concerns the untap step, phasing, turn-based actions, controlling another player, and one-shot "until" effects ([502.3], [502.4], [703.4a], [610.4a], etc.) — none of them address counters, replacement effects on entering the battlefield, or ability-removal layers. The net result matches controlling no artifact at all [Phylactery Lich ruling #0].
- Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Humility onto the battlefield simultaneously [Genesis Wave ruling #5], and Humility removes all creature abilities [Humility ruling #1], which would strip Phylactery Lich's indestructible and its "When you control no permanents with phylactery counters on them, sacrifice this creature" state trigger [Phylactery Lich ruling #2] [Phylactery Lich ruling #4]. The exact layer/timestamp interaction for the "as enters" ability is not covered by anything I was given.

What's missing from my context: rules on counters and permanents that can't receive them, replacement effects that apply as a permanent enters, and the layer system for ability-removing continuous effects.

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so it reads the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Avery controls [The One Ring] and casts [Teferi's Protection] then casts a second The One Ring. What happens at the start of the next turn?
answer:
Honest correction: the Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not cover this question. They deal with suspend (702.62a–d, 116.2f), casting permissions (601.3), sorcery/instant timing (307.5, 307.5a, 304.5), spell ownership and control (112.2a), opponents making choices (601.7, 602.3), controlling another player (723.5a), and the suspected designation (701.60b). None of those address phasing, phase-in timing, protection from everything, or the legend rule, so I can't ground the outcome in the numbered rules provided.

What the provided card data does support (without any numbered rule behind it): Teferi's Protection's own text says Avery's permanents "phase in before you untap during your untap step," and its rulings say a phased-out permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist, phases in with its counters, and doesn't retrigger enters-the-battlefield abilities [Teferi's Protection ruling #5, Teferi's Protection ruling #15, Teferi's Protection ruling #20, Teferi's Protection ruling #21]. That tells you the first The One Ring returns at Avery's untap step and that the second The One Ring won't re-grant protection. But the key step — what happens when two legendary permanents named The One Ring are on the battlefield at once — is the legend rule, and no rule text covering it was provided, so I'm not going to assert it as a grounded conclusion here.

To settle it properly you'd need the rules on phasing (702.25) and the legend rule (704.5j).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.113.7a: The source of an ability is the object that generated it. The source of an activated ability on the stack is the object whose ability was activated. The source of a triggered ability (other than a delayed triggered ability) on the stack, or one that has triggered and is waiting to be put on the stack, is the object whose ability triggered. To determine the source of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f. Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability. Note that some abilities cause a source to do something (for example, “This creature deals 1 damage to any target”) rather than the ability doing anything directly. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. Otherwise, it will check that information when it resolves. In both instances, if the source is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.
gold_text.502.1: First, all phased-in permanents with phasing that the active player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that the active player controlled when they phased out phase in. This all happens simultaneously. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. See rule 702.26, “Phasing.”
gold_text.503.1a: The upkeep step has no turn-based actions. Once it begins, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.”) Any abilities that triggered during the untap step and any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesn’t matter. (See rule 603, “Handling Triggered Abilities.”)

question: Amaya controls [Dralnu, Lich Lord], [Furnace of Rath] and six [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico casts [Incinerate] targeting Dralnu, Lich Lord. If Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath, how many other permanents will they need to sacrifice?
answer:
Five other permanents — Furnace of Rath plus five of the six Snow-Covered Forests (six permanents total), assuming Amaya applies Furnace of Rath's doubling effect first.

Why: Incinerate would deal 3 damage to Dralnu, Lich Lord. Two replacement effects want to modify that event: Furnace of Rath ("it deals double that damage") and Dralnu, Lich Lord's own "If damage would be dealt to Dralnu, sacrifice that many permanents instead." When two replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected object's controller — Amaya, as controller of Dralnu, Lich Lord — chooses the order [616.1f]. Applying Furnace of Rath first turns 3 damage into 6, then Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect replaces that damage with sacrificing 6 permanents. Amaya controls 8 permanents (Dralnu, Lich Lord, Furnace of Rath, six Snow-Covered Forests), so 6 is payable; sacrificing Furnace of Rath is allowed and Dralnu, Lich Lord itself could even be one of them [Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #4]. Sacrificing Furnace of Rath as part of the payment does not shrink the requirement — the doubling was already locked in when the replacement was applied.

Note on the other ordering: if Amaya instead applies Dralnu, Lich Lord's replacement first, the damage event is replaced by sacrificing only 3 permanents, and there is no damage left for Furnace of Rath to double [616.1f, Furnace of Rath ruling #4]. That would be just 2 other permanents besides Furnace of Rath. The question's framing implies the doubled (6-permanent) ordering.

Also: Incinerate's "can't be regenerated" clause is irrelevant here, since Dralnu, Lich Lord is never actually dealt damage. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Two or five, Amaya's choice.

As Amaya is the controller of the affected object, Amaya will choose which order to apply the replacement effects in. If Amaya chooses to apply Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, the 3 damage will be converted into sacrificing three permanents, and Furnace of Rath will no longer apply to that event since there's no longer any damage being dealt. If they chooses to apply Furnace of Rath first, then the three damage will be doubled to six damage, and then will be replaced by sacrificing six permanents.

Whether Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath or not is irrelevant, as all replacement effects are applied to the event before anything is actually sacrificed.

question: Nicolas controls [Razorfield Thresher], [Lake of the Dead], and [Veinfire Borderpost]. Aubrey controls [Omniscience] and casts [Casualties of War], choosing Razorfield Thresher as the artifact target and the creature target. Then they cast [Radiate], targeting Casualties of War. What will be destroyed after all spells and abilities have resolved?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules text provided to me in this conversation does not settle this question. The numbered rules I was given cover companion ([702.139a], [702.139b], [702.139c], [103.2b], [116.2g]), APNAP order ([101.4b]), drawing with an empty library ([121.3a]), conspiracies ([315.5a]), partner ([702.124f], [702.124m]), archenemy first turn ([904.6]), choosing card names ([201.4f]), Two-Headed Giant setup ([805.3b]), and the initiative ([726.5]). None of those address modal spells, targeting legality, or how copies made by Radiate choose their targets.

What the provided card data does support, on its own:
- Casualties of War is modal and Aubrey may choose several modes but not the same mode twice ([Casualties of War ruling #0]), so the "Destroy target artifact" and "Destroy target creature" modes were each chosen once, both aimed at Razorfield Thresher, which is an artifact creature.
- When Casualties of War resolves, its targets are destroyed in the order printed, and any abilities that trigger from those destructions wait until Casualties of War finishes resolving ([Casualties of War ruling #1]).
- Omniscience lets Aubrey cast both spells without paying mana costs, but normal timing permissions still apply ([Omniscience ruling #1]).
- Lake of the Dead's sacrifice-a-Swamp effect only applies when Lake of the Dead would enter the battlefield ([Lake of the Dead ruling #0]), so it does not interact here; Veinfire Borderpost's alternative cost ([Veinfire Borderpost ruling #1]) also never comes up.

What is missing: I was given no rule (and no Radiate ruling) covering (a) whether a spell with two targeting instances aimed at the same permanent counts as one that "targets only a single permanent or player," and (b) how a copy's targets must be legal when the copy's modes require both an artifact and a creature target. Those two points are exactly what decides whether Radiate produces any copies, and therefore whether anything besides Razorfield Thresher is destroyed. Without rules on spell copies and target legality (the 601.2 and 706/707 material), I can't ground a full answer.

I also can't say from the provided rules how the answer would differ at a multiplayer table versus two players, since no multiplayer targeting rules were provided.

question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. What the given material does say, and which cuts against the intended loop: [Clone ruling #5] states that if the creature Clone copies is itself copying something else, Clone enters as whatever that creature copied, and [Spark Double ruling #7] says the same for Spark Double. So Clone's copy choice resolves to an original copiable object rather than chaining freely, and [Spark Double ruling #3] only tells us that a Spark Double copying a creature enters with one +1/+1 counter plus counters from abilities it copied. Nothing provided authorizes re-applying the inherited replacement effect repeatedly to the same enters-the-battlefield event, and nothing provided forbids it either, so I can't give you a number without guessing.

For reference, Clone's own ability grants no counter; only Spark Double's ability adds one. So the count would equal the number of times Spark Double's ability is legally applied to that single entry event — exactly the point the missing rules would decide.

question: Arabella casts [Mind's Desire]. In response, Neil casts [Lim-Dûl's Vault]. How many copies of Mind's Desire are created when the storm trigger resolves?
answer:
The number of copies is unchanged by Neil's spell: storm counts only spells cast **before** Mind's Desire earlier that turn, and Lim-Dûl's Vault was cast afterward (in response). So if Mind's Desire was the first spell cast that turn, zero copies are created; if two spells had already been cast that turn before it, two copies, and so on.

Details:
- Storm reads "When you cast this spell, copy it for each spell cast before it this turn." Lim-Dûl's Vault is cast after Mind's Desire, so it is not counted [Mind's Desire ruling #3 confirms which spells count — spells from any zone and even countered spells count, but they must have been cast before Mind's Desire].
- Neil casting Lim-Dûl's Vault in response puts it on the stack above the storm trigger, so it will resolve first; its shuffling and reordering of Neil's library has no effect on the count or on Arabella's copies. Arabella's own Mind's Desire shuffles her library and exiles her top card only when the spell (or a copy) actually resolves.
- Each copy is put directly onto the stack rather than cast, and copies aren't counted by later storm spells [707.10b, Mind's Desire ruling #4]. Each copy carries the same choices as the original [707.10b], and each copy shuffles Arabella's library and exiles a card that she may play without paying its mana cost as it resolves; the card is exiled face up [Mind's Desire ruling #0], and if unplayed by end of turn it stays exiled [Mind's Desire ruling #1].
- The storm trigger itself can be countered, which would produce no copies at all [Mind's Desire ruling #2], and copies must be countered individually [Mind's Desire ruling #5].

This works the same whether there are two players or more: only the timing of casts relative to Mind's Desire matters, and spells cast by any player earlier in the turn count.

question: Ainsley activates [Priest of Forgotten Gods]'s ability, but doesn't choose a target for the first part. Can Nickolas respond to the ability?
answer:
Yes — Nickolas can respond. My basis is the card's own rulings, not the Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided: none of the numbered rules given to me here (they cover Two-Headed Giant life totals, paying life, cumulative upkeep, lifelink, afflict, increment, proliferate) address mana abilities, the stack, or priority, so the numbered rules text in this context does not settle the question on its own.

What does settle it is the authoritative ruling on the card: because the ability of Priest of Forgotten Gods may have targets, it is not a mana ability; it uses the stack and can be responded to, even if no targets were chosen [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #1]. Ainsley may legally activate it choosing no targets, and Ainsley will still add {B}{B} and draw a card on resolution [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #0].

question: Nayeli controls a [Yixlid Jailer]. Ariel has a [Golgari Brownscale] in their graveyard and returns it to their hand with [Disturbing Plot]. Does Ariel gain 2 life?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: Ariel does not gain 2 life.

But I should be plain about what that rests on. None of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (they cover storm, gravestorm, myriad, copying spells and abilities, linked abilities, shuffling, layers, and how many times a triggered ability triggers) address Yixlid Jailer's effect, graveyard-functioning abilities, or leave-the-graveyard triggers. So I cannot ground this in a numbered rule from the provided text.

What does settle it is the card text and rulings provided, which the instructions treat as authoritative grounding:

- Yixlid Jailer reads "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." Golgari Brownscale, sitting in Ariel's graveyard, therefore has no abilities there.
- Golgari Brownscale's ability is "When this card is put into your hand from your graveyard, you gain 2 life." Its trigger condition is about leaving the graveyard, so the ability has to be functioning while Golgari Brownscale is still in the graveyard.
- [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4] establishes exactly this line: an ability whose trigger event happens while the card is in (or entering) the graveyard "triggers from the graveyard," and Yixlid Jailer "stops those abilities from triggering at all." [Yixlid Jailer ruling #6] draws the contrast: only abilities that trigger on leaving the battlefield trigger from the battlefield and so escape Yixlid Jailer.

So when Disturbing Plot resolves and returns Golgari Brownscale from Ariel's graveyard to Ariel's hand (Disturbing Plot returns the card to its owner's hand), there is no life-gain ability present to trigger. Golgari Brownscale regains its abilities once it is in Ariel's hand, but the trigger event has already passed.

[Golgari Brownscale ruling #0] confirms the ability would otherwise trigger on any return from graveyard to hand, not just via dredge — that just isn't enough with Yixlid Jailer on the battlefield. If Ariel had conspired Disturbing Plot, the copy behaves the same way for any other creature card returned from a graveyard.

Yixlid Jailer affects cards in every player's graveyard, so this result is the same at a two-player table and at a multiplayer one.

question: Aryana has taken control of an [Ahn-Crop Crasher] from Noe with [Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded], which Aryana exerts. After Aryana ends their turn, will it untap during Noe's untap step?
answer:
Yes — Ahn-Crop Crasher will untap during Noe's untap step.

I want to be transparent about my grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided in this conversation (707.10 and its subrules, 115.7e/f, 201.5b, 608.2f, 614.9, 702.144a, 120.4c/d, 801.5a, 801.13a, 707.11) address exert, untap steps, or control-change duration. So I am not citing any numbered rule. What does settle it is the card data I was given, which is authoritative on its own.

Exert means that as you declare a creature as an attacker you may choose to have it attack with a bonus effect, at the cost that it won't untap during your next untap step. Ahn-Crop Crasher's own text says an exerted creature "won't untap during your next untap step" — that is, the untap step of the player who exerted it, Aryana. Aryana's control of Ahn-Crop Crasher via Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded's −6 ability lasts only until end of turn, so Ahn-Crop Crasher reverts to Noe's control. Noe's untap step is not Aryana's untap step, so Ahn-Crop Crasher untaps normally. This is precisely the situation covered by Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #4: if you gain control of another player's creature until end of turn and exert it, it will untap during that player's untap step. Aryana's exert would only bite if Aryana somehow controlled Ahn-Crop Crasher again at Aryana's own next untap step.

This outcome doesn't depend on the player count: with two players or more, it's Noe's own untap step, whenever it arrives in turn order, at which Ahn-Crop Crasher untaps.

answer_gold: Yes. A player exerting a permanent only causes it to not untap during that player's next untap step, not any untap step that would untap it.

question: Andres controls [Strionic Resonator] and plays [Clive's Hideaway]. They activate Strionic Resonator targeting the hideaway trigger, exiling 2 cards. On their next turn, they activate Clive's Hideaway's ability to cast the exiled card. What happens as it resolves?

Both exiled cards can be played without paying their mana costs, provided Andres controls four or more legendary creatures as Clive's Hideaway's ability resolves.

- Clive's Hideaway's hideaway trigger is linked to its "{2}, {T}: You may play the exiled card without paying its mana cost if you control four or more legendary creatures" ability. Copies of a linked triggered ability are also linked to that second ability, and "the exiled card" then refers to all cards exiled by the trigger and the copy [Strionic Resonator ruling #1], with the ability getting multiple answers when it asks about "the exiled card" [Strionic Resonator ruling #3].
- So on the later turn, one activation of Clive's Hideaway's ability lets Andres play both exiled cards for free, in any order (or fewer, since it says "may") [Strionic Resonator ruling #3].

Cost note: the activation cost is {2} generic plus tapping Clive's Hideaway; exiling two cards doesn't change it. The four-legendary-creatures condition is part of the effect, checked on resolution. Nothing here depends on player count, so the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Aspen controls [Cosima, God of the Voyage] and mutates [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt] onto it, putting it underneath Cosima, God of the Voyage. At the beginning of their next upkeep, Aspen exiles Cosima, God of the Voyage to its own triggered ability. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Aspen's whole mutated permanent leaves the battlefield and goes to exile, and both physical cards — Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt — end up in exile as two separate cards. Cosima, God of the Voyage's ability then grants the exiled Cosima, God of the Voyage card the "Whenever a land you control enters" ability, which lets Aspen stack voyage counters or return it.

Why: the permanent on the battlefield was a single merged permanent represented by two cards (Cosima, God of the Voyage on top, Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt underneath). The only merged-permanent rule provided here is [712.21c], for melded permanents: one permanent leaves the battlefield but two cards are put into the appropriate zone, and an effect that can find the new object finds both cards, taking the same action on each. Applying that same principle, the exile instruction moves both cards to exile.

Caveats you should act on:
- The exile happens only if the mutated permanent is still on the battlefield as the upkeep ability resolves; Cosima, God of the Voyage's ability triggers only if it was on the battlefield at the beginning of upkeep [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #13].
- Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's "whenever this creature mutates" trigger already happened back when the mutate spell resolved; exiling later does nothing further with it [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt ruling #0].
- While in exile, when a land Aspen controls enters, the granted ability triggers; on resolution it checks that Cosima, God of the Voyage is still exiled, and if it has left exile the ability does nothing [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #11]. Declining to add a voyage counter returns Cosima, God of the Voyage to the battlefield with X +1/+1 counters and draws X cards, X = voyage counters; you may return it with zero counters [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #5].
- What I can't settle from the provided rules: the specific mutate rules (how the merged permanent's cards separate, and whether the return-from-exile effect brings back only the Cosima, God of the Voyage card or is treated as finding both cards) are not in the context. Under the [712.21c] analogy the return effect would find both cards; without the actual mutate rule I can't confirm that for a mutated (rather than melded) permanent. Note also that anything returning is a new object [603.7c].
- Multiplayer: nothing here changes between two players and more, except that if Aspen were to leave a multiplayer game, a triggered ability they would control isn't put on the stack, so the return would never happen [800.4d].
