gold_text.201.5a: Text that refers to the object it’s on by name means just that particular object and not any other objects with that name, regardless of any name changes caused by game effects. If an ability’s effect grants another ability to an object, and that second ability refers to that first ability’s source by name, the name refers only to the specific object which is that first ability’s source. The second ability does not refer to any other object with the same name as the first ability’s source. However, if the second ability also moved the first ability’s source to a different public zone, the name refers to the object the source became in its new zone. This is also true if the second ability is copied onto a new object. Gutter Grime has an ability that reads “Whenever a nontoken creature you control dies, put a slime counter on this enchantment, then create a green Ooze creature token with ‘This token’s power and toughness are each equal to the number of slime counters on Gutter Grime.’” The ability granted to the token only looks at the Gutter Grime that created the token, not at any other Gutter Grime on the battlefield. A copy of that token would also have an ability that referred only to the Gutter Grime that created the original token.
gold_text.729.3: Because each player draws seven cards when a game begins, any player with fewer than seven cards in their deck will lose the subgame when state-based actions are checked during the upkeep step of the first turn, regardless of any mulligans that player takes. (See rule 704, “State-Based Actions.”)

cited_text.712.21c: If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone. If an effect can find the new object that a melded permanent becomes as it leaves the battlefield, it finds both cards. (See rule 400.7.) If that effect causes actions to be taken upon those cards, the same actions are taken upon each of them. Otherworldly Journey is an instant that reads “Exile target creature. At the beginning of the next end step, return that card to the battlefield under its owner’s control with a +1/+1 counter on it.” A player casts Otherworldly Journey targeting Chittering Host, a melded permanent. Chittering Host is exiled. At the beginning of the next end step, Midnight Scavengers and Graf Rats are both returned to the battlefield, each with a +1/+1 counter on it. False Demise is an Aura with the ability “When enchanted creature dies, return that card to the battlefield under your control.” A Chittering Host enchanted by False Demise dies. The triggered ability returns both Midnight Scavengers and Graf Rats to the battlefield. Mimic Vat is an artifact that reads, in part, “Whenever a nontoken creature dies, you may exile that card.” A Chittering Host dies. As Mimic Vat’s triggered ability resolves, its controller makes a single choice and both cards that represented Chittering Host are either exiled or not.
cited_text.603.7c: An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time. A delayed triggered ability will contain “when,” “whenever,” or “at,” although that word won’t usually begin the ability. A delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects it even if the object changes characteristics. However, if that object is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at the time the delayed triggered ability resolves, the ability won’t affect it. (Note that if that object left that zone and then returned, it’s a new object and thus won’t be affected. See rule 400.7.) An ability that reads “Exile this creature at the beginning of the next end step” will exile the permanent even if it’s no longer a creature during the next end step. However, it won’t do anything if the permanent left the battlefield before then.
cited_text.800.4d: Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game. If an object that would be owned by a player who has left the game would be created in any zone, it isn’t created. If a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game would be put onto the stack, it isn’t put on the stack. Astral Slide is an enchantment that reads, “Whenever a player cycles a card, you may exile target creature. If you do, return that creature to the battlefield under its owner’s control at the beginning of the next end step.” During Alex’s turn, Bianca uses Astral Slide’s ability to exile Alex’s Hypnotic Specter. Before the end of that turn, Bianca leaves the game. At the beginning of the end step, the delayed triggered ability generated by Astral Slide that would return Hypnotic Specter to the battlefield triggers, but it isn’t put on the stack. Hypnotic Specter never returns to the battlefield.

answer_gold:
Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt both get exiled and gain the corresponding triggered ability. 

The ability on Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt still refers to Cosima, God of the Voyage in exile, so whenever a land enters the battlefield under Aspen's control, they can choose to put up to 2 counters on Cosima, God of the Voyage, and if they chooses not to for both triggers, they'll draw twice that many cards.

question: Aubrey controls [Whiskervale Forerunner] and casts [Growth Cycle] to give it +3/+3. Before it resolves, Aubrey casts [Cooperate] choosing to copy Growth Cycle and changes the target to another creature. Does Whiskervale Forerunner trigger again?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: No — Whiskervale Forerunner does not trigger a second time.

Honesty note on grounding: the Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover suspend, special actions, split second, priority and instant/sorcery timing — they do not contain any rule about valiant, targeting, or copying spells. So the substance of this answer rests on the card text and the provided card rulings (which are authoritative grounding), not on the numbered rules. The only numbered rules that bear on the situation are the priority rules: Aubrey may cast the Cooperate half of Refuse // Cooperate as an instant while Growth Cycle is still on the stack, because a player may cast an instant any time they have priority [117.1a], [304.1].

The reasoning from card text and rulings:
- Whiskervale Forerunner's own text reads "Whenever this creature becomes the target of a spell or ability you control for the first time each turn..." Growth Cycle targeting Whiskervale Forerunner was that first time, so the valiant ability has already triggered for the turn, and it resolves before Growth Cycle does [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #2].
- Cooperate targets the instant or sorcery spell it copies (Growth Cycle), not Whiskervale Forerunner, so casting Cooperate doesn't target Whiskervale Forerunner.
- The copy is put onto the stack rather than cast [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #11], and Aubrey changed its target to another creature [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #18], so Whiskervale Forerunner never becomes the copy's target either.
- Even had the copy stayed on Whiskervale Forerunner, it wouldn't trigger, since a copy triggers valiant only if the creature hasn't already been targeted by a spell or ability you control this turn [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #1].
- The copy resolves before the original Growth Cycle [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #14], and each Growth Cycle's bonus is locked in as it begins to resolve [Growth Cycle ruling #1].

A different creature newly targeted by the copy would trigger its own valiant ability if it has one and hasn't been targeted this turn. Nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.707.10c: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. Some effects copy a spell or ability and state that its controller may choose new targets for the copy. The player may leave any number of the targets unchanged, even if those targets would be illegal. If the player chooses to change some or all of the targets, the new targets must be legal. Once the player has decided what the copy’s targets will be, the copy is put onto the stack with those targets.

cited_text.117.1a: Unless a spell or ability is instructing a player to take an action, which player can take actions at any given time is determined by a system of priority. The player with priority may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions. A player may cast an instant spell any time they have priority. A player may cast a noninstant spell during their main phase any time they have priority and the stack is empty.
cited_text.304.1: A player who has priority may cast an instant card from their hand. Casting an instant as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”)

answer_gold: No. When copying spells that allow the copies controller to change the target, the targets are changed before the spell is put onto the stack. There is never a point in time where the spell is targeting Whiskervale Forerunner before the targets are changed.

question: Nico has a [Pillarfield Ox] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Arjun casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nico. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nico know which manifested card is which?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged): the three +1/+1 counters remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, so it comes back as a face-down 5/5, and Nico will be able to identify it for that reason.

But I want to be plain about my grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me (602.2, 602.3, 602.3b, 602.5c, 701.2a, 723.3, 723.5a, 723.9, 804.2, 109.4a, 112.2a, 113.6j, 113.8, 118.12, 613.1b) address counters, zone changes, manifest, or face-down permanents. They are about activating abilities, controlling a player, and determining controllers. So I am not resting this answer on any numbered rule, and I won't invent one. My grounding is entirely the card text and the provided card rulings, which the instructions treat as authoritative:

- Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own printed text: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." This card text overrides the general rule that counters vanish on a zone change. Ghastly Conscription moves the card graveyard → exile → battlefield; neither is a hand or library, so the counters ride along.
- [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]: the ability only works if Skullbriar has it in the zone it's moving from — it does in the graveyard and in exile.
- [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #0]: those counters aren't "placed," they merely remain.
- [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]: power/toughness counters apply in zones other than the battlefield too.
- [Ghastly Conscription ruling #8]: the manifested permanent is a 2/2 with no name, mana cost, types, or abilities — so with three +1/+1 counters it's a 5/5, versus the manifested Pillarfield Ox at 2/2. That defeats the shuffle intended to hide identities per [Ghastly Conscription ruling #3], so Nico can tell which is which.
- [Ghastly Conscription ruling #13]: Arjun, who manifested them, may look at his own face-down permanents; Nico may not, but can deduce from the counters.
- [Ghastly Conscription ruling #2]: Arjun may turn the Skullbriar card face up any time he has priority by revealing it and paying its mana cost {B}{G} — a special action that doesn't use the stack.
- [Ghastly Conscription ruling #6]: if Arjun leaves the game, Nico's card is exiled.

Caveat from [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]: while face down the permanent has no abilities, so if it leaves the battlefield still face down it would lose the counters.

This is the same in a two-player game or multiplayer; Ghastly Conscription just targets one player's graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.122.2: Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another. The counters are not “removed”; they simply cease to exist. See rule 400.7.
gold_text.406.3: Exiled cards are, by default, kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time. Cards “exiled face down” can’t be examined by any player except when instructions allow it. However, if a player is instructed to look at a card and then exile it face down, or once a player is allowed to look at a card exiled face down, that player may continue to look at that card until it leaves the exile zone or is part of a pile of cards that are shuffled, even if the instruction allowing the player to do so no longer applies.

answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nico will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Pillarfield Ox.

question: Avery activates [Ascendant Spirit]'s first ability. Before it resolves Avery casts [Slip Out the Back] targeting Ascendant Spirit. When it phases back in, what will it look like?
answer:
Point taken on the citation check: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given ([903.x] Commander/Brawl deck construction, [702.139x]/[103.2b] companion, [608.3e] permanent spell resolution, [707.9f] copy effects, [702.124m] partner) say anything about phasing, activated abilities resolving, or setting base power and toughness. So the numbered rules text does not settle this question. My answer rests entirely on the card rulings supplied for Slip Out the Back and Ascendant Spirit, which are themselves authoritative grounding and do directly cover this interaction.

On that basis, the answer stands: Ascendant Spirit phases back in as a 1/1 Snow Creature — Spirit with a +1/+1 counter on it, i.e. a 2/2 Spirit, and the {S}{S} ability accomplishes nothing.

- Phasing out means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist until it phases in [Slip Out the Back ruling #1], so when the first ability resolves there is no Ascendant Spirit for it to turn into a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3. The mana spent is not refunded.
- The counter placed by Slip Out the Back survives, because a permanent that had counters when it phased out has them when it phases back in, during its controller's untap step; it can attack and pay {T} that turn [Slip Out the Back ruling #2].
- Counters that modify power and toughness apply on top of base power and toughness [Ascendant Spirit ruling #4], giving 2/2.
- Phasing in causes no "enters the battlefield" triggers [Slip Out the Back ruling #3].

Timing assumption: the ability was activated, then Slip Out the Back was cast and resolved first (it was put on the stack later, so it resolves first). If instead the {S}{S} ability had already resolved before Slip Out the Back was cast, Ascendant Spirit would be a Spirit Warrior with base 2/3, losing its other creature types [Ascendant Spirit ruling #3]; that effect has no duration and lasts until Ascendant Spirit leaves the battlefield or another effect changes it [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8], and phasing out is not leaving the battlefield, so it would phase back in as a 2/3 Spirit Warrior with the +1/+1 counter = 3/4.

Nothing in this depends on the player count, and no multiplayer rule was provided that would change it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.26e: Phasing If a continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability modifies the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects, a phased-out permanent won’t be included in the set of affected objects. This includes continuous effects that reference the permanent specifically, unless they also specifically refer to the permanent as phased out.

answer_gold: It will be a 2/2 and not a Warrior. When Ascendant Spirit's ability resolves it's phased out and won't be affected.

question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
answer:
No. Aspen must apply Parallel Lives first, and only then the devour replacement effects of the tokens.

Why: creating a token is the outer event, and a permanent entering the battlefield is an event contained within that creation event. When one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer one must be chosen first — so Parallel Lives (which replaces the number of tokens created) is applied before any "as this enters" replacement effect such as devour on the resulting tokens [616.1g]. Parallel Lives doubles the tokens: unkicked Rite of Replication makes 1 token, so 2 tokens; kicked (the additional {5}) it makes 5, so 10 tokens [Parallel Lives, Rite of Replication].

Then each token that's a copy of Caldera Hellion has its own devour 1, and each one's "as this creature enters" ability works on the token [Rite of Replication ruling #11]. But sacrificing one creature cannot feed all of them: the same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how permanents enter the battlefield [614.13b], and a creature you already control can be devoured by only one of several simultaneously-entering devour creatures [Caldera Hellion ruling #3]. So one sacrificed creature gives exactly one token a single +1/+1 counter; every other token enters with none. To give each token a counter you'd need one separate already-on-battlefield creature per token, and none of the entering tokens can be devoured, nor can a token devour itself [Caldera Hellion ruling #1]. All creatures devoured this way are sacrificed at the same time [Caldera Hellion ruling #3].

Note also that each token then triggers "deals 3 damage to each creature," and a token with only one +1/+1 counter (4/4) still dies to the combined damage from multiple tokens [Caldera Hellion ruling #4].

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; if more than two players are at the table and multiple players had simultaneous replacement choices, those choices would be made in APNAP order [616.1g].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.616.1g: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). While following the steps in 616.1a–f, one replacement or prevention effect may apply to an event, and another may apply to an event contained within the first event. In this case, the second effect can’t be chosen until after the first effect has been chosen. A player is instructed to create a token that’s a copy of Voice of All, which has the ability “As this creature enters, choose a color.” Doubling Season has an ability that reads “If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead.” Because entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, the effect of Doubling Season must be applied first, and then the effects of the two Voice of All tokens may be applied in either order.
gold_text.616.2: A replacement or prevention effect can become applicable to an event as the result of another replacement or prevention effect that modifies the event. One effect reads “If you would gain life, draw that many cards instead,” and another reads “If you would draw a card, return a card from your graveyard to your hand instead.” Both effects combine (regardless of the order they came into existence): Instead of gaining 1 life, the player puts a card from their graveyard into their hand.

cited_text.616.1g: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). While following the steps in 616.1a–f, one replacement or prevention effect may apply to an event, and another may apply to an event contained within the first event. In this case, the second effect can’t be chosen until after the first effect has been chosen. A player is instructed to create a token that’s a copy of Voice of All, which has the ability “As this creature enters, choose a color.” Doubling Season has an ability that reads “If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead.” Because entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, the effect of Doubling Season must be applied first, and then the effects of the two Voice of All tokens may be applied in either order.
cited_text.614.13b: An effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield may cause other objects to change zones. The same object can’t be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield. Jund (a plane card) says, “Whenever a player casts a black, red, or green creature spell, it gains devour 5.” A player controls Runeclaw Bear and casts Thunder-Thrash Elder, a red creature spell with devour 3. As Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield, its controller can choose to sacrifice Runeclaw Bear when applying the devour 3 effect or when applying the devour 5 effect, but not both. Thunder-Thrash Elder will enter the battlefield with zero, three, or five +1/+1 counters, depending on this choice.

answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Caldera Hellion: Caldera Hellion's own effect and Parallel Lives's effect. Caldera Hellion's effect applies to it entering the battlefield however, while Parallel Lives's effect applies to it being created, so Parallel Lives's effect must be applied first. After that is applied the original Caldera Hellion's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Caldera Hellions entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged): Aubrey's Exotic Orchard produces no mana — it cannot be tapped for anything here.

Important transparency point: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules provided to me in this conversation address mana, mana abilities, or colors of mana. Those provided rules are all about controllers of objects and abilities ([110.2a], [113.8], [109.4a], [109.4b], [603.3a], [603.7e], [111.2], [302.2], [303.4e], [610.3c], [613.1b], [703.2], [103.1c]) and none of them bear on this question. So my answer does not rest on any numbered rule.

What it does rest on is the card data and rulings supplied, which are authoritative on their own:
- Exotic Orchard: "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce."
- [Exotic Orchard ruling #3]: "The colors of mana are white, blue, black, red, and green. Exotic Orchard can't be tapped for colorless mana, even if a land an opponent controls could produce colorless mana."
- Crumbling Vestige's activated mana ability is "{T}: Add {C}", and {C} is colorless mana specifically, not a color and not generic.

Since Crumbling Vestige's ongoing ability produces only {C}, there is no color for Exotic Orchard to copy, so Aubrey's Exotic Orchard yields nothing. Crumbling Vestige's "When this land enters, add one mana of any color" is a one-time enters-the-battlefield trigger rather than something Crumbling Vestige can do repeatedly; [Exotic Orchard ruling #0] and [Exotic Orchard ruling #1] confirm Exotic Orchard ignores costs and restrictions and cares only about colors, which still doesn't convert {C} into a color.

If any opponent controls a land that could produce a color (a Forest, for instance), Exotic Orchard could be tapped for that color. With only Aubrey and Nikolas, only Nikolas's lands matter; at a multiplayer table Exotic Orchard checks every opponent's lands, so another player's colored-mana land would enable it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.106.7: Some abilities produce mana based on the type of mana another permanent or permanents “could produce.” The type of mana a permanent could produce at any time includes any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time, taking into account any applicable replacement effects in any possible order. Ignore whether any costs of the ability could or could not be paid. If that permanent wouldn’t produce any mana under these conditions, or no type of mana can be defined this way, there’s no type of mana it could produce. Exotic Orchard has the ability “{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce.” If your opponent controls no lands, activating Exotic Orchard’s mana ability will produce no mana. The same is true if you and your opponent each control no lands other than Exotic Orchards. However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.

answer_gold: Any color. Exotic Orchard checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: yes, Azariah can see which player was secretly chosen for Stalking Leonin.

On your point about sourcing: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (they cover flying, reach, changeling, copy effects, linked abilities, permanent status, double-faced permanents, and enters-the-battlefield replacement effects) address controlling another player or hidden information. So I am not citing any numbered rule, because doing so would be inventing one. What does settle this question is the authoritative card rulings supplied in the context:

- Azariah controls Beckham as a player and therefore sees all cards in the game that Beckham can see, including Beckham's hidden information [Worst Fears ruling #11].
- The secretly chosen opponent for Stalking Leonin is recorded as hidden information kept with the card, e.g. that player's name written on a piece of paper kept with Stalking Leonin [Stalking Leonin ruling #2]. That is information Beckham has access to, so Azariah sees it.

Supporting details from the same rulings: Azariah makes all of Beckham's choices and decisions that turn, including whether to activate abilities [Worst Fears ruling #1], using only Beckham's resources for Beckham's costs [Worst Fears ruling #8]; Azariah controls the player only, not Beckham's permanents [Worst Fears ruling #4]; and Beckham remains the active player [Worst Fears ruling #7]. Practically, Stalking Leonin's ability requires a creature attacking Beckham controlled by the chosen player, and a creature attacking a planeswalker Beckham controls doesn't qualify [Stalking Leonin ruling #4] — during Beckham's own turn there usually won't be a legal target. Azariah still can't view Beckham's sideboard or cards outside the game [Worst Fears ruling #12], and can't make choices Beckham wouldn't be called on to make [Worst Fears ruling #2].

Three-player vs. two-player: identical answer; with Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan the only difference is that the secret choice could have been Azariah or Caelan, and Azariah learns which.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.722.4: In every zone, a preparation card has only its normal characteristics.

answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules text I was given does not settle this. The numbered rules provided to me are all about damage, lifelink, life totals, exchanging/doubling life, and Two-Headed Giant life sharing ([120.3f], [120.4c], [120.4d], [702.15b], [702.15e], [702.15f], [119.3], [701.10d], [701.12c], [810.9], [810.9a], [810.9d], [904.5]). None of them cover banding, declaring attackers in a band, the legend rule, or copy effects, so I can't ground a banding ruling in the rules text supplied.

What the provided card data does say (offered as context, not as a substitute for the missing banding rules):
- Master of the Hunt's tokens are named Wolves of the Hunt and have "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," and its reminder text says bands are formed from creatures named Wolves of the Hunt, at least one of which has that ability.
- Sakashima the Impostor's copy effect states that its name remains Sakashima the Impostor, and [Sakashima the Impostor ruling #2] confirms the name is not copied. So neither Sakashima the Impostor is named Wolves of the Hunt.
- Mirror Gallery ([Mirror Gallery ruling #0]) only turns off the legend rule; it doesn't change names.

That suggests only one attacking creature (the actual Wolves of the Hunt token) qualifies as a band member by name, which would leave no legal band — but confirming how bands are declared, and whether a creature with the banding ability can band with differently named creatures, requires the banding rules (rule 702.21 and the declare-attackers rules), which were not provided here. Please supply those rules for a definitive answer.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.22c: Banding As a player declares attackers, they may declare that one or more attacking creatures with banding and up to one attacking creature without banding (even if it has “bands with other”) are all in a “band.” They may also declare that one or more attacking [quality] creatures with “bands with other [quality]” and any number of other attacking [quality] creatures are all in a band. A player may declare as many attacking bands as they want, but each creature may be a member of only one of them. (Defending players can’t declare bands but may use banding in a different way; see rule 702.22j.)

answer_gold: No bands can be declared. The only creature on the battlefield named "Wolves of the Hunt" is the token, so it cannot declare itself as in a band with anything else. The Sakashima the Impostor with "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt" is not itself named "Wolves of the Hunt", so it cannot declare itself as in a band with the token.

question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
answer:
The Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not cover phasing at all, so I can't fully settle this from the provided context. None of the supplied rules (state-based actions, look-back-in-time triggers, ending the turn, players leaving the game, tribute, bloodthirst, poison counters, creatures put onto the battlefield attacking, etc.) address when permanents phase out or in, what happens to Auras attached to a permanent that phases out, or how tokens behave when they phase out.

What the card text alone tells you: Teferi's Curse says "Enchanted permanent has phasing. (It phases in or out before its controller untaps during each of their untap steps. While it's phased out, it's treated as though it doesn't exist.)" Phasing is the mechanic where a permanent flips between existing normally ("phased in") and being treated as though it doesn't exist ("phased out"). Reading only that reminder text, the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter — each enchanted by one of Nadia's Teferi's Curses — would phase out during Avery's untap step, since a given permanent phases either in or out once per that step and both are currently phased in.

But the questions of (a) whether the two Teferi's Curses themselves phase out along with the permanents they enchant, (b) whether Barbed Bloodletter remains attached to the Germ token, (c) whether a token that phases out returns when it phases in, and (d) exactly which later untap step they phase in on, all require the phasing rules (rule 702.26) and the token rules, which are not in the context I was given. I'm not going to guess at those from memory.

I'm also assuming both Teferi's Curses are attached before Avery's untap step begins; if one were attached later, that permanent wouldn't have phased out this turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.26d: Phasing The phasing event doesn’t actually cause a permanent to change zones or control, even though it’s treated as though it’s not on the battlefield and not under its controller’s control while it’s phased out. Zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Tokens continue to exist on the battlefield while phased out. Counters and stickers remain on a permanent while it’s phased out. Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

answer_gold: All 4 permanents will phase out and phase back in in Ari's next untap step. Barbed Bloodletter and both Teferi's Curses will still be attached to the permanents they were attached to previously. Phasing doesn't cause tokens to cease to exist or unattach permanents from other permanents.

question: Alessandra controls [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse]. During their main phase, they cast [Day's Undoing]. How much life does each player gain/lose?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: nobody gains or loses life — Alessandra gains 0 and each opponent loses 0.

Honest sourcing note: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover this interaction. Every numbered rule in my context concerns phasing and "until"-phasing one-shot effects ([502.1], [702.26a]–[702.26i], [610.4]–[610.4c], [703.4a], [110.5c], [603.10b], [722.3c]), and none of them address drawing cards, ending the turn, or triggered abilities ceasing to exist. So I cannot cite a numbered rule here, and I am not going to invent one.

What my answer does rest on is the card data provided, which the ground rules treat as authoritative: [Day's Undoing ruling #5] states that if any abilities trigger while players are shuffling cards into their library or drawing seven cards, those abilities cease to exist when the turn ends and won't be put on the stack. Sheoldred, the Apocalypse's "Whenever you draw a card, you gain 2 life" and "Whenever an opponent draws a card, they lose 2 life" trigger on the seven draws each player makes from Day's Undoing, but because Day's Undoing then ends Alessandra's turn, those triggers never reach the stack and never resolve. [Day's Undoing ruling #4] confirms that in the end-the-turn process no player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack.

Assumed timing: Alessandra cast Day's Undoing during their own main phase, so the "If it's your turn, end the turn" clause applies. If instead it resolved on another player's turn, the turn would not end, the triggers would resolve normally, and Alessandra would gain 14 life while each opponent lost 14 (Alessandra choosing the order of simultaneous triggers per [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse ruling #0]).

Multiplayer: the result is the same with two players or more — no opponent loses any life regardless of how many there are.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.723.1a: Some cards allow a player to control another player during that player’s next turn. This effect applies to the next turn that the affected player actually takes. The affected player is controlled during the entire turn; the effect doesn’t end until the beginning of the next turn. Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works.

answer_gold: None. The players first draw seven cards each, triggering Sheoldred, the Apocalypse fourteen times. Then Alessandra ends the turn, which nullifies those triggers before they're even put onto the stack.

question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules text provided to me does not settle this question. Every numbered rule I was given ([119.3], [119.5], [119.7], [119.8], [701.10d], [701.12c], [701.12g], [810.9] and its subrules [810.9a], [810.9c], [810.9d], [810.9f], [810.9g], [810.9h], and [904.5]) concerns life totals, life gain/loss, exchanging or doubling life, Two-Headed Giant shared life totals, and Archenemy starting life. None of them address day/night, daybound/nightbound, transforming permanents, copy effects, battles, or defense counters — the things this question turns on.

What is missing from my context: the rules on transforming double-faced permanents and which face is up, the daybound/nightbound rules, the copy rules for copying a card in a graveyard, and the battle/defense-counter rules. Without those numbered rules I won't assert a full resolution from memory.

For what it's worth, the card rulings I was given point in a direction but do not close the loop on their own: Lazotep Convert copies exactly what was printed on the copied creature card [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #12], [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #13], so a copy of Kessig Naturalist would have daybound; daybound permanents transform as it becomes night, immediately and not as a state-based action [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #2]; battles only receive defense counters as they enter the battlefield [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #4], and a battle with no defense counters is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action without triggering the Siege's exile-and-cast ability [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #9], [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #14]. But no provided rule tells me which face a transform actually turns this specific permanent to while a copy effect is applying, so I'm flagging this as unresolved rather than guessing.

A judge or the actual daybound/transform/copy sections of the Comprehensive Rules would be needed to confirm.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.110.5: A permanent’s status is its physical state. There are four status categories, each of which has two possible values: tapped/untapped, flipped/unflipped, face up/face down, and phased in/phased out. Each permanent always has one of these values for each of these categories.
gold_text.702.145b: Daybound and Nightbound Daybound is found on the front faces of some double-faced cards and represents three static abilities. “Daybound” means “If it is night and this permanent is represented by a double-faced card, it enters transformed,” “As it becomes night, if this permanent is front face up, transform it,” and “This permanent can’t transform except due to its daybound ability.” See rule 731, “Day and Night.”
gold_text.707.2: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, “{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.” Clone is a creature that reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.” After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can’t pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.

answer_gold: Lazotep Convert will be a copy of Kessig Naturalist. As it becomes night, it will not transform and remain a copy of Kessig Naturalist. Lazotep Convert will only copy the front face of Kessig Naturalist and does not copy its status. When it becomes night, it will not transform because a daybound permanent will only transform as it becomes night if it is front face up. ([702.145b])

question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
answer:
Short answer: the provided rules don't settle this, so I won't state a definitive yes or no.

What is clear from the context:

- Fireblade Charger's ability is "When this creature dies, it deals damage equal to its power to any target," so the damage is dealt by Fireblade Charger itself, not by Adelina, and the amount is set from Fireblade Charger's last known existence on the battlefield ([Fireblade Charger ruling #0]). If its power there was 0 or less, the ability does nothing regardless of Thwart the Enemy.
- Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nasir casts Thwart the Enemy in response to the death trigger, so Thwart the Enemy resolves and sets up its prevention effect before Fireblade Charger's triggered ability resolves. If instead Thwart the Enemy were cast after the damage had already been dealt, it could do nothing about that damage — a prevention effect can only apply to damage not yet dealt.
- Prevention is a replacement-type effect applied as the damage event would occur ([616.1f] governs how such effects are chosen and applied when more than one applies).

What's missing: Thwart the Enemy prevents damage "dealt this turn by creatures your opponents control," and by the time the ability resolves, Fireblade Charger is in Adelina's graveyard. [400.7h] tells us a card that changes zones becomes a new object with no relation to its previous existence, but the provided rules do not include the rule on last known information / how a source that has left the battlefield is treated for the purpose of a "creatures your opponents control" restriction. The one ruling given only addresses the power value, not control. Without that rule in context, I can't ground a firm answer.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on player count — Thwart the Enemy affects creatures controlled by all of Nasir's opponents, so the analysis is identical whether Adelina is Nasir's only opponent or one of several.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.113.7a: The source of an ability is the object that generated it. The source of an activated ability on the stack is the object whose ability was activated. The source of a triggered ability (other than a delayed triggered ability) on the stack, or one that has triggered and is waiting to be put on the stack, is the object whose ability triggered. To determine the source of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f. Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability. Note that some abilities cause a source to do something (for example, “This creature deals 1 damage to any target”) rather than the ability doing anything directly. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. Otherwise, it will check that information when it resolves. In both instances, if the source is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.

cited_text.400.7h: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions. If an effect allows a nonland card to be cast, other parts of that effect can find the new object that card becomes after it moves to the stack as a result of being cast this way.
cited_text.616.1f: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply. Two permanents are on the battlefield. One is an enchantment that reads “If a card would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it,” and the other is a creature that reads “If this creature would die, instead shuffle it into its owner’s library.” If the creature is destroyed, its controller decides which replacement to apply first; the other does nothing. Essence of the Wild reads “Creatures you control enter as a copy of this creature.” A player who controls Essence of the Wild casts Rusted Sentinel, which normally enters the battlefield tapped. As it enters the battlefield, the copy effect from Essence of the Wild is applied first. As a result, it no longer has the ability that causes it to enter the battlefield tapped. Rusted Sentinel will enter the battlefield as an untapped copy of Essence of the Wild.

answer_gold: Unclear. Fireblade Charger is not currently a creature on the battlefield, but the game uses its last known information to determine how the damage is dealt. If Fireblade Charger only applies to objects that are creatures, like how Biomantic Mastery only counts creatures that actually exist on the battlefield, it won't be prevented. But if Fireblade Charger checks the source of damage to see whether it's a creature, it will be able to identify the damage as coming from a creature. The intention is probably the latter, but Wizards has not clarified.

question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: after Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls Corrupted Conscience, and because Corrupted Conscience says "You control enchanted creature," Analia also controls Bane Alley Blackguard. Nico controls neither.

Grounding, stated honestly: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me are about control-changing effects or Auras — they cover replacement effects that modify how permanents enter the battlefield (616.1f/616.1g, 614.12, 614.13b, 707.5, 707.9b, 611.2e, 712.13a, 712.21c, 701.24g, 603.6a, 113.6h) and keyword-instance rules (702.123b, 702.135b, 702.149b). So I am not citing any of those; they don't bear on this question.

What does settle it is the card text plus the provided ruling, which are authoritative on their own:
- Lay Claim: "Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent." Corrupted Conscience is a permanent (an Aura enchantment), so Lay Claim can enchant it and gives control of it to Lay Claim's controller, Analia.
- Lay Claim ruling #0 states the governing principle for the "you" in an Aura's text: "an Aura's effect that affects 'you' still affects its controller." Corrupted Conscience's effect is "You control enchanted creature," so that "you" is now Analia, the new controller of Corrupted Conscience. Hence Analia controls Bane Alley Blackguard.

Analia's ownership of Bane Alley Blackguard doesn't matter here; control is determined by the effect. Bane Alley Blackguard also still has infect from Corrupted Conscience.

Note the direction: Analia got Corrupted Conscience by targeting it directly with Lay Claim, not by gaining control of the creature — per Lay Claim ruling #0, merely gaining control of a creature would not have given her the Aura.

This result is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players, and no multiplayer-specific rule was provided.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.1b: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 2: Control-changing effects are applied.
gold_text.613.7: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp.
gold_text.613.7a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. A continuous effect generated by a static ability has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later. If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same. Rune of Flight is an Aura that grants enchanted Equipment “Equipped creature has flying.” A player attaches Rune of Flight to Colossus Hammer, an Equipment with “Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying.” The ability granted by Rune of Flight shares Rune of Flight’s timestamp because it is later than Colossus Hammer’s timestamp. If Colossus Hammer becomes attached to a creature, both of its abilities receive new timestamps (see rule 613.7e), but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same.
gold_text.613.7e: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. An Aura, Equipment, or Fortification receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object or player.
gold_text.613.8a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect is said to “depend on” another if (a) it’s applied in the same layer (and, if applicable, sublayer) as the other effect; (b) applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to; and (c) neither effect is from a characteristic-defining ability or both effects are from characteristic-defining abilities. Otherwise, the effect is considered to be independent of the other effect.
gold_text.613.8b: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied. If multiple dependent effects would apply simultaneously in this way, they’re applied in timestamp order relative to each other. If several dependent effects form a dependency loop, then this rule is ignored and the effects in the dependency loop are applied in timestamp order.

answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

question: Autumn controls [Traveling Chocobo] and casts [Phyrexian Ingester]. Autumn exiles [Scarwood Goblins] and then [Tor Giant] with the triggers. What are Phyrexian Ingester's power and toughness?
answer:
Phyrexian Ingester ends up 5/5 — and only one creature actually gets exiled, so the scenario's second exile shouldn't happen.

Grounding: my answer rests mainly on the card text and rulings provided, plus one rule from the provided Comprehensive Rules text.

1. Traveling Chocobo's third ability applies only when "a land or Bird you control entering the battlefield causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger" [Traveling Chocobo]. Phyrexian Ingester is a Creature — Phyrexian Beast, neither a land nor a Bird, so its Imprint "when this creature enters" trigger is not given an extra instance. It triggers once, and Autumn exiles one nontoken creature — Scarwood Goblins, a 2/2.
2. Phyrexian Ingester then gets +X/+Y where X and Y are the exiled creature card's power and toughness [Phyrexian Ingester]. Those values are read off the card in the exile zone; counters, Auras, and Equipment it had while on the battlefield don't count [Phyrexian Ingester ruling #1], and only power/toughness-defining (characteristic-defining) abilities apply in exile, not ones that add or subtract [Phyrexian Ingester ruling #2]. Rule [208.2a] backs this up: a characteristic-defining ability that sets power and/or toughness "functions everywhere, even outside the game." Scarwood Goblins has no such ability and is simply 2/2, so the bonus is exactly +2/+2 — making Phyrexian Ingester 3/3 + 2/2 = 5/5. Tor Giant is never exiled in this line.
3. Counterfactual: if Phyrexian Ingester's trigger somehow did trigger twice and both Scarwood Goblins (2/2) and Tor Giant (3/3) were exiled, "the exiled creature card" would get multiple answers and they'd be summed [Traveling Chocobo ruling #8], giving +5/+5 for an 8/8. Also, Traveling Chocobo never copies a trigger — it just adds an instance, with targets chosen separately per instance [Traveling Chocobo ruling #11].

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players, except that in Two-Headed Giant Traveling Chocobo's doubling doesn't apply to a teammate's permanents [Traveling Chocobo ruling #6].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.607.3: If, within a pair of linked abilities, one ability refers to a single object as “the exiled card,” “a card exiled with [this object],” or a similar phrase, and the other ability has exiled multiple cards (usually because it was copied), the ability refers to each of the exiled cards. If that ability asks for any information about the exiled card, such as a characteristic or mana value, it gets multiple answers. If these answers are used to determine the value of a variable, the sum of the answers is used. If that ability performs any actions on “the” card, it performs that action on each exiled card. If that ability creates a token that is a copy of “the” card, then for each exiled card, it creates a token that is a copy of that card. If that ability performs any actions on “a” card, the controller of the ability chooses which card is affected.

cited_text.208.2a: Rather than a fixed number, some creature cards have power and/or toughness that includes a star (*). The card may have a characteristic-defining ability that sets its power and/or toughness according to some stated condition. (See rule 604.3.) Such an ability is worded “[This creature’s] [power or toughness] is equal to . . .” or “[This creature’s] power and toughness are each equal to . . .” This ability functions everywhere, even outside the game. If the ability needs to use a number that can’t be determined, including inside a calculation, use 0 instead of that number. Lost Order of Jarkeld has power and toughness each equal to 1+*. It has the abilities “As this creature enters, choose an opponent” and “Lost Order of Jarkeld’s power and toughness are each equal to 1 plus the number of creatures the chosen player controls.” While Lost Order of Jarkeld isn’t on the battlefield, there won’t be a chosen player. Its power and toughness will each be equal to 1 plus 0, so it’s 1/1.

answer_gold:
It's an 8/8.

The enter-the-battlefield ability of Phyrexian Ingester is part of a pair of linked abilities. When determining a value for Phyrexian Ingester's second ability, the sum of the powers and toughnesses from Scarwood Goblins and Tor Giant is used. This gives Phyrexian Ingester +5/+5, which makes it an 8/8.

question: Beverly controls [Pandemonium]. Adalynn casts [Knight Errant] and targets Beverly's [Forest Bear] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Channing casts [Ral's Outburst] targeting Adalynn causing them to lose the game. Will Beverly's creature die?
answer:
Honest correction: the Comprehensive Rules text provided to me in this conversation does not settle this question. Every numbered rule I was given (106.5, 106.6, 106.7, 106.9–106.12b, 305.6, 605.2, 605.4a, 712.5f) concerns mana production, mana abilities, basic land types, and meld pairs. Nothing in that provided rules text addresses a player leaving the game, what happens to abilities on the stack or permanents they controlled, who controls a triggered ability from an enchantment, or how damage from an ability is determined when its source has left the battlefield. So I cannot ground a rules-based answer here, and I'm setting answered to false rather than citing rules from memory.

What the provided card data does say, for what it's worth: Pandemonium's ability is controlled by Beverly, the controller of Pandemonium, even though Knight Errant entered under Adalynn's control and Adalynn chose the target (Beverly's Forest Bear) and whether to deal damage [Pandemonium ruling #1]. And Pandemonium's ability doesn't check power until it resolves; if the creature isn't on the battlefield then, it deals damage equal to the power it had immediately before leaving the battlefield [Pandemonium ruling #0]. Read together, those rulings point toward Knight Errant's ability still resolving for 2 damage and killing the 2/2 Forest Bear. But the crucial step — that Adalynn losing the game to Channing's Ral's Outburst removes Knight Errant and Adalynn's objects while leaving Beverly's trigger on the stack — is not covered by any rule I was given, so treat that as unconfirmed here.

Timing note: I assumed Channing's Ral's Outburst was cast in response to the Pandemonium trigger and so resolved first. Also note this is a three-player situation, and I was given no multiplayer rules text at all.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.603.3a: Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority. See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.” The ability becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has the text of the ability that created it, and no other characteristics. It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere. A triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered, unless it’s a delayed triggered ability. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f.
gold_text.608.2d: If the object that’s resolving is an instant spell, a sorcery spell, or an ability, its resolution may involve several steps. The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last. If an effect of a spell or ability offers any choices other than choices already made as part of casting the spell, activating the ability, or otherwise putting the spell or ability on the stack, the player announces these while applying the effect. question: Asher casts [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Asher wants to put [Hall of Triumph] onto the battlefield. Do they know what Noa is putting onto the battlefield while making the choice for Hall of Triumph's replacement effect?
answer:
Direct answer: No — not necessarily. Asher makes the color choice for Hall of Triumph after every player has chosen their card, but Noa is not required to reveal what they chose, so Asher may know only *which* card Noa picked, not what it is.

How the resolution goes: Show and Tell's card choices are made during its resolution, not on announcement, and Asher (the active player) chooses first, then each other player in turn order [Show and Tell ruling #1] [Show and Tell ruling #2]. A player doesn't have to reveal the chosen card so long as it's clear which physical card was chosen, and after all choices are made the cards are put onto the battlefield simultaneously [Show and Tell ruling #2].

Hall of Triumph says "As Hall of Triumph enters, choose a color," which is an "as ... enters" choice made as the permanent enters, not a separate later action; such choices are made after all players have chosen their cards, with the active player making choices for their card first, then the other players in turn order [Show and Tell ruling #0] [613.2a]. So Asher chooses Hall of Triumph's color knowing that Noa has locked in a card and can no longer change it — but if Noa left it face down/unrevealed, Asher must pick the color blind as to its identity. If Noa's card is revealed or otherwise known, Asher does get to use that information, since the color choice happens after all card choices.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players the same ordering applies — all players choose cards in turn order starting with the active player, then "as enters" choices are made by the active player first and the remaining players in turn order [Show and Tell ruling #0] [Show and Tell ruling #2]. So Asher, as active player, always makes the Hall of Triumph color choice before any other player makes choices for their own entering permanents, whether the table is two players or more.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying.

Why: Tightening Coils says the enchanted creature "gets -6/-0 and loses flying." That "loses flying" is a one-time-applied continuous effect whose position relative to other ability-granting effects is set by timestamp. Reattaching Fleetfeather Sandals to Wandering Ones gives Fleetfeather Sandals's grant of flying and haste a new, later timestamp than Tightening Coils, so flying is granted after Tightening Coils takes it away. This is exactly the situation covered by [Tightening Coils ruling #0]: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature will have flying.

Note the -6/-0 is unaffected — that's a power-changing effect applied in layer 7 ([613.1g]), and it doesn't compete with the flying question. Wandering Ones (a 1/1) ends up with power 1-6 = -5 and toughness 1, but it does have flying (and haste from Fleetfeather Sandals), so it can attack or block as a flier — it just deals no combat damage with 0-or-less power.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Tightening Coils became attached before this turn's equip activation, as stated. If instead Tightening Coils were attached after Fleetfeather Sandals's most recent attachment, Tightening Coils would have the later timestamp and Wandering Ones would not have flying.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

question: Addilynn activates the Unearth ability of their [Extractor Demon], returning it to the battlefield. Before their end step, Addilynn casts [Reality Ripple] targeting Extractor Demon. What happens to it?
answer:

answer_gold: Extractor Demon phases out. When the unearth trigger resolves during Addilynn's end step, it won't be exiled. It will phase back in during Addilynn's next untap step, after which point it will be exiled instead of being put anywhere else if it would leave the battlefield.

question: Avery controls [Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher] and Natalie controls [Verity Circle] and [Koskun Falls]. Avery attacks Natalie with Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, and then taps it to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls. Will Natalie's Verity Circle trigger?
answer:
Yes — Natalie's Verity Circle triggers, and Natalie may draw a card.

Why: Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher has vigilance, so being declared as an attacker doesn't tap it. Avery then activates Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's own ability, whose cost is {T}, to add {C} equal to Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's toughness in order to pay the {2} that Koskun Falls demands for each attacking creature. That mana restriction ("can't be spent to cast spells from your hand") doesn't matter here, because paying Koskun Falls' attack cost isn't casting a spell.

So Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher actually changes from untapped to tapped, and it is not being tapped as part of being declared as an attacker — it's tapped for its mana ability while already attacking. That is precisely the case covered by [Verity Circle ruling #2]: a creature with vigilance declared as an attacker that then becomes tapped while attacking does trigger Verity Circle. Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher is a creature an opponent (Avery) controls from Natalie's perspective, so the trigger condition is met. The draw is optional ("you may draw a card").

Caveats on the requirements: the trigger needs a real untapped-to-tapped change ([Verity Circle ruling #1]) — if Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher were somehow already tapped, no trigger. Timing note: I'm assuming, as stated, that Avery taps Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher for mana after it has been declared as an attacker. If instead you imagine mana being produced before attackers are declared, Verity Circle still triggers for the same reason (the tap isn't a declaration-as-attacker tap) — either ordering gives Natalie the trigger.

Multiplayer: this works the same at any table size; Koskun Falls only taxes creatures attacking its controller, so only Avery's creatures attacking Natalie cost {2} each. In Two-Headed Giant the tax is still only once per attacking creature ([Koskun Falls ruling #0]). Also note Koskun Falls is a world enchantment, so if another world permanent enters, the world rule ([704.5k], [Koskun Falls ruling #1]) can put Koskun Falls into Natalie's graveyard.

question: Nico controls [Platinum Emperion]. Alexandra attacks with [Hopeful Eidolon], which Nico doesn't block. Does Alexandra gain life?
answer:
Yes — Alexandra gains 1 life, and Nico's life total does not change. But I want to be transparent about the basis: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (they cover sacrifice, offering, emerge, devour, annihilator, casualty, resolution steps, etc.) address lifelink, damage, or life gain at all. The only provided grounding for this interaction is the card data and rulings.

What the provided card material says:
- Hopeful Eidolon is a 1/1 Spirit with lifelink: "Damage dealt by this creature also causes you to gain that much life." Unblocked, it deals 1 combat damage to Nico.
- Platinum Emperion reads "Your life total can't change," which restricts only its controller, Nico.
- [Platinum Emperion ruling #3] settles the case directly: Platinum Emperion's ability doesn't prevent damage, it changes the result of that damage, and the example given is exactly this one — "if a creature with lifelink deals damage to you, you won't lose any life, but its controller will still gain that much life."

So Hopeful Eidolon's damage is still dealt to Nico (and would still trigger anything that triggers on damage being dealt to Nico, per [Platinum Emperion ruling #4]), Nico's life total stays put, and Alexandra gains 1 life.

Since Platinum Emperion's text limits only its own controller's life total, this outcome is identical in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing in the provided material makes the player count matter here. I'm assuming ordinary combat damage in the combat damage step with no other effects involved.

answer_gold:
Yes. Damage can have 0 or more results. Normally a creature with lifelink dealing damage to a player would have two results:

* Its controller gains that much life.
* The recipient of the damage loses that much life.

Platinum Emperion makes the second result impossible, so only the first occurs.

question: Atlas attacks with [Pristine Angel], and Nico targets it with [Cephalid Snitch] before blockers. After combat, Atlas casts a spell, untapping Pristine Angel. Once untapped, can Nico target it with [Mob]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can target Pristine Angel with Mob, and Mob will destroy it.

Why: Pristine Angel's ability reads "As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color." Once Atlas casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel, that ability turns back on, so Pristine Angel again has protection from each color — including black — from its own ability. But Cephalid Snitch's resolved effect ("Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn") is a continuous effect that lasts for the rest of the turn, and it has a later timestamp than Pristine Angel's static ability. Applying them in timestamp order (rule 613.7c), Pristine Angel ends up with protection from artifacts and from every color except black. The Cephalid Snitch effect isn't "used up" when Pristine Angel is tapped; it keeps applying to whatever protection Pristine Angel has for the duration.

So Mob, a black instant, is a legal choice of target, and its "Destroy target creature" resolves normally. (Note that even against protection from black, protection would only have prevented the targeting/damage side of things — here it doesn't matter, since the protection from black is gone.)

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability resolved this same turn, before Pristine Angel was untapped, so its "until end of turn" effect is still active. If the untap happened on a later turn, or after the Cephalid Snitch effect had expired at end of turn, Pristine Angel would have full protection from black while untapped and could not be targeted by Mob.

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on the number of players — the same answer applies whether it's a two-player game or a larger table, since Mob targets a single creature and Nico is choosing that target.

An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. Each counter receives a timestamp as it’s put on an object or player. If that object or player already has a counter of that kind on it, each counter of that kind receives a new timestamp identical to that of the new counter.

question: Ashley controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 1 [Bayou]. Naomi controls a [Reverence] and 3 Bayous. Can Ashley attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
No — Ashley can't attack Naomi with Gaea's Liege (it could still attack a planeswalker Naomi controls, if she had one).

A note on grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided in this conversation all concern playing lands (rules 305.x, 701.18a, 400.7h/i, 101.2, etc.) and none of them address combat, declaring attackers, or characteristic-defining power/toughness. So I am not citing any numbered rule; this answer rests entirely on the card text and the provided rulings, which are authoritative grounding on their own.

Reasoning from that card data:
- Gaea's Liege reads "As long as Gaea's Liege isn't attacking, its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests you control," and [Gaea's Liege ruling #0] states that when being declared as an attacker you use the "not attacking" power and toughness — it only changes after declaration is complete.
- Ashley controls one Bayou, which is a "Land — Swamp Forest," so it has the Forest land type; [Bayou ruling #0] confirms that things affecting basic land types do apply to it even though it isn't a basic land. That's 1 Forest, so Gaea's Liege has power 1 at the moment of declaration.
- Reverence reads "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you." Power 1 is 2 or less, so Gaea's Liege can't be declared as an attacker against Naomi. Naomi's 3 Bayous would have made Gaea's Liege 3/3 while attacking, but that value only applies after declaration, which never legally occurs.
- Per [Reverence ruling #0], Reverence only protects Naomi herself, so Gaea's Liege could legally attack a planeswalker Naomi controls.

Aside: Gaea's Liege's "{T}: Target land becomes a Forest until this creature leaves the battlefield" could raise Ashley's Forest count, but it requires tapping Gaea's Liege, so it couldn't attack that turn anyway. question: Ares controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. Nico controls a [Contamination]. If Ares taps the Gaea's Cradle, what mana is produced, if any?
answer:
Nothing — no mana at all. I want to be transparent about my grounding: the Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover tokens, meld, and replacement effects that modify how permanents enter the battlefield, and none of them address mana production or the amount of mana a land makes. So this answer rests entirely on the two cards' own text plus the provided Contamination rulings, which are authoritative on their own.

Gaea's Cradle reads "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control." Ares controls no creatures, so the amount is zero. Contamination reads "If a land is tapped for mana, it produces {B} instead of any other type and amount," and the ruling clarifies that effects which generate mana based on some count are "affected in color but not in amount" [Contamination ruling #2]. Since Gaea's Cradle produces zero mana, there is nothing for Contamination to recolor: Ares gets no {G} and no {B}, and has simply tapped Gaea's Cradle for nothing.

Contamination's second ability is a replacement effect, not a triggered ability [Contamination ruling #0], so it applies at the instant Gaea's Cradle is tapped with no window to respond in between. Nothing here depends on player count, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — Contamination applies to any land tapped for mana. If Ares controlled one creature instead, Gaea's Cradle would produce one mana and Contamination would make it {B} rather than {G}.
