See rule 605, “Mana Abilities.” A replacement effect that applies if a permanent “is tapped for mana” or tapped for mana of a specific type and/or amount modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana or the specified type and/or amount of mana.

answer_gold: No mana is produced. Gaea's Cradle is not producing any mana, so Contamination's replacement effect doesn't apply.

question: Aubrey controls a [Necromancy] that was cast during their declare blockers step. During Aubrey's end step, Nikolai activates [Duskmantle Guildmage]'s first ability. Does Aubrey lose 1 life when the Necromancy is sacrificed?
answer:
Honest answer: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not settle this question. The provided rules cover damage processing (120.1a, 120.4c), umbra armor (702.89a), wither (702.80b, 702.80d), shadow, afflict, annihilator, color-changing (105.3), some state-based actions (704.5f, 704.5v), end-the-turn/end-the-combat-phase procedures (724.1c, 724.2c), prevention shields (609.7b), and multiplayer range of influence (801.13a). None of them address the cleanup step's timing, delayed triggered abilities, "this turn" duration, or cards being put into a graveyard triggering life loss — the pieces this question actually turns on.

What the card text and rulings I was given do say, for what it's worth: Necromancy's own text states that if it's cast when a sorcery couldn't have been cast (as here, during Aubrey's declare blockers step), "the controller of the permanent it becomes sacrifices it at the beginning of the next cleanup step," and [Necromancy ruling #4] confirms the sacrifice happens only because Necromancy was cast using its own flash-granting ability. Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability reads "Whenever a card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere this turn, that player loses 1 life," and [Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #1] notes it does not trigger for token permanents, while [Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #0] notes multiple activations each trigger separately and [Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #2] notes it applies to each of Nikolai's opponents (so two-player and multiplayer play alike, provided Aubrey is Nikolai's opponent). That text points toward Aubrey losing 1 life when the Necromancy card is put into Aubrey's graveyard, plus possibly another 1 life if the reanimated creature card is then sacrificed to Necromancy's leaves-the-battlefield ability.

But confirming that the cleanup step still counts as part of "this turn" for Duskmantle Guildmage's delayed trigger, and that such a trigger can actually be put on the stack and resolve during the cleanup step, requires rules that were not provided to me. I'd need the rules on the cleanup step and on delayed triggered abilities to answer definitively.

question: Alma casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Nico's [Bronze Sable]. In response, Nico casts [Brute Strength] on the Bronze Sable. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
I have to walk back my previous answer: the Comprehensive Rules text provided to me here does not settle this question. The rules I was given are all about paying costs (702.137a spectacle, 601.2h, 118.3, 118.5, 118.7, 118.12, 118.13c, 113.2b, 113.6j, 508.1j, 509.1f, 609.4b, 614.17b). - what happens to a creature whose toughness becomes 0 or less (the state-based action that puts it into the graveyard),

What I can ground: the Virulent Wound card text creates a delayed trigger, "When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter," and [Virulent Wound ruling #0] states that if the creature is not put into a graveyard on the turn Virulent Wound resolves, its controller won't get a poison counter. So whether Nico gets a poison counter depends entirely on whether Bronze Sable is put into a graveyard during that same turn — and the provided rules text gives me nothing to establish whether the loss of Brute Strength's bonus at end of turn causes Bronze Sable's death within that turn.

I'm also assuming the order stated in the question: Alma casts Virulent Wound targeting Bronze Sable, Nico casts Brute Strength on Bronze Sable in response, so Brute Strength resolves first and Virulent Wound second. Under the opposite order the same gap in the provided rules would remain.

To answer this properly I'd need the rules on continuous effects lasting "until end of turn," the state-based action for 0-or-less toughness, and the cleanup step.

question: Angelina controls [Ice Cauldron]. Noel controls [Suppression Field]. Angelina activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Angelina's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?

Direct answer unchanged: Angelina adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana, spendable only to cast the card last exiled with Ice Cauldron.

I should be transparent about grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me (they cover tournament rules, zones, the command zone, and casual variants) address this interaction at all. My answer rests entirely on the two cards' own printed text plus their provided rulings, which are authoritative grounding in their own right.

From the card text and rulings:
- Suppression Field: "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities." So Ice Cauldron's first ability cost {X} + {2}; with X=1 that's three mana, paid as {C}{C}{C}.
- Ice Cauldron's first ability says to "note the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost" — the mana actually spent, not the value of X. Ice Cauldron ruling #8 confirms the Cauldron counts only mana spent and doesn't see X, so the note is {C}{C}{C}, and that is what the second ability adds.
- Activating the second ability is not taxed: it's a mana ability (Ice Cauldron ruling #0), and Suppression Field exempts mana abilities (Suppression Field ruling #0). Its cost is just {T} plus removing a charge counter.
- The mana is restricted: spend it only on the last card exiled with Ice Cauldron (Ice Cauldron ruling #13). Angelina may add other mana to finish the cost (Ice Cauldron ruling #5), and may cast the exiled card only when she could legally cast it normally (Ice Cauldron ruling #3).

Player count doesn't change this; Suppression Field taxes every player's non-mana activated abilities, including Noel's. If you want a Comprehensive Rules citation for the cost-modification math itself, that rules text wasn't included in my context.

question: Ariel activates [Warped Landscape]. Before that resolves Noe casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Ariel is resolving Warped Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
answer:
Yes — Ariel can cast Panglacial Wurm from their library during that search, paying its full mana cost {5}{G}{G}.

Why:
- Panglacial Wurm says "While you're searching your library, you may cast this card from your library." Warped Landscape's second ability says "Search your library for a basic land card," and it is Ariel's own library, so the ability applies [Panglacial Wurm ruling #6].
- Aven Mindcensor changes the search so that Ariel (an opponent of Noe) searches only the top four cards of their library instead. That still counts as searching that library [Aven Mindcensor ruling #0], and Panglacial Wurm is among those top four here, so Ariel sees it and may cast it [Aven Mindcensor ruling #2].
- Timing: Ariel must cast Panglacial Wurm before finding any card with the search effect [Panglacial Wurm ruling #1]. Casting it follows all normal casting rules except for timing and zone; the spell goes on the stack, and Ariel can activate mana abilities while casting it, which resolve immediately without using the stack [Panglacial Wurm ruling #0], [605.3b].
- A Panglacial Wurm cast this way can't then be found by Warped Landscape's search [Panglacial Wurm ruling #4] — so Ariel still finds a basic land card (from the top four only), puts it onto the battlefield tapped, and shuffles [Aven Mindcensor ruling #1]. While searching, Ariel must keep the library in the same order until the shuffle [Panglacial Wurm ruling #2].
- After Warped Landscape's ability finishes resolving, the active player gets priority with Panglacial Wurm on the stack, and any cast-triggers go on the stack then [Panglacial Wurm ruling #3].

If Ariel has enough mana, multiple Panglacial Wurms could be cast during this one search [Panglacial Wurm ruling #5].

Player count doesn't change this: Aven Mindcensor restricts any opponent of Noe who searches, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game (in multiplayer it would equally restrict any other opponent of Noe).

Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated. (See rule 405.6c.)

question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: The Copy Artifact stops being a Dance of the Dead and becomes a 6/4 copy of Streetbreaker Wurm (still keeping the {1}{U}{R} copy ability). Because it never left the battlefield, Dance of the Dead's leaves‑the‑battlefield trigger never triggers, so the Viashino Warrior is NOT sacrificed — it simply loses the +1/+1 (back to 4/2) and loses the "doesn't untap" restriction, and the Copy Artifact becomes unattached from it since it's no longer an Aura.

Step by step:

1. Mycosynth Lattice makes every permanent an artifact, so Dance of the Dead, Streetbreaker Wurm and everything else on the battlefield are artifacts [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1].
2. While March of the Machines was on the battlefield, each noncreature artifact (including the Aura Dance of the Dead, mana value 2) was an artifact creature with power/toughness equal to its mana value. Normally an Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything and would be unattached and then put into the graveyard by state‑based actions [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3]. That never happens here, because everything in the question occurs during Eureka's single resolution — cards put onto the battlefield by Eureka aren't cast, and anything that triggers waits until resolution is complete [Eureka ruling #2, Eureka ruling #3] — and March of the Machines is sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked before Eureka finishes. Note: the exact rule governing when state‑based actions are checked isn't in the provided context, so I'm relying on Eureka ruling #3 for the timing that nothing happens mid‑resolution.
3. The Copy Artifact entered as a copy of the Mizzium Transreliquat, and results of copy effects are copied, so it got Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} ability the Transreliquat's second ability grants, and it is an enchantment in addition to its other types [Copy Artifact ruling #3, Copy Artifact ruling #2, Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #0, Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3]. Sakashima's own copy ability then let it enter instead as a copy of Dance of the Dead (which was a creature at that moment thanks to March of the Machines); Sakashima copies only printed/copiable values, so a copied "creature that's not normally a creature" isn't a creature — the Copy Artifact is a Dance of the Dead Aura, not a 2/2 [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #0, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #1].
4. That Dance of the Dead trigger resolves, putting Viashino Warrior onto the battlefield tapped under Alvin's control and attaching the Copy Artifact to it, giving it +1/+1 (5/3) and "doesn't untap during its controller's untap step" [Dance of the Dead ruling #1].
5. Alvin then activates the {1}{U}{R} ability targeting Streetbreaker Wurm (a legal target because Mycosynth Lattice makes it an artifact). The Copy Artifact becomes a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm, except it has that ability. Copiable values don't include the +1/+1 the original Streetbreaker Wurm is getting from Alvin's other Dance of the Dead (that's a layer‑7 non‑copy effect), so it's a 6/4 [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #1, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #1, 613.1g].
6. Consequences: the Copy Artifact no longer has Dance of the Dead's text at all, so the +1/+1 and the untap restriction on Viashino Warrior are gone (4/2, and it will untap normally), and it is no longer an Aura so it can't stay attached. Crucially, Dance of the Dead's sacrifice clause only triggers "when this Aura leaves the battlefield"; the permanent stayed on the battlefield, so Viashino Warrior survives. Alvin's original Dance of the Dead on Streetbreaker Wurm is untouched, and Streetbreaker Wurm remains a 7/5 (6/4 plus +1/+1).

One genuinely unsettled point: whether the "except it's an enchantment in addition to its other types" clause from Copy Artifact still applies after the new copy ability overwrites its copy status isn't answered by the rules/rulings provided, so I can't state that with certainty; either way it's an artifact (Mycosynth Lattice) creature copy of Streetbreaker Wurm.

Player count doesn't change any of this — everything involved is Alvin's own permanents. The only multiplayer difference is Eureka's own loop, which continues around all players until every player in sequence declines [Eureka ruling #0].

question: Aspen controls a [Blood Tyrant] that they took control of from Briella using [Malevolent Whispers]. Aspen has 1 life. Cason casts [Volt Charge] targeting Aspen. After it resolves and Aspen loses the game, will Blood Tyrant get the +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Honest correction: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given settle this question. The provided rules text covers multiple instances of keyword abilities triggering separately (702.191b, 702.116b, 702.105b, 702.149b, 702.108b, 702.134b, 702.15e, 702.154d, 702.130b), abilities that trigger additional times (603.2d), replacement effects not invoking themselves (614.5), loyalty-cost combination (606.5), characteristic layers (613.1a), and entering-the-battlefield replacement effects (614.13b). None of those address a player losing the game, state-based actions for a life total of 0 or less, what happens when a player leaves a multiplayer game, or how a control-change effect like Malevolent Whispers ends — the things this question actually turns on. So I'm setting answered to false rather than dressing up outside knowledge with an unrelated citation.

What I can say on the provided card material alone: [Blood Tyrant ruling #1] states that Blood Tyrant's third ability triggers no matter how a player loses the game, expressly including losing as a state-based action from having a life total of 0 or less. Aspen at 1 life taking 3 damage from Volt Charge is exactly that case, so on the strength of that ruling Blood Tyrant's "Whenever a player loses the game, put five +1/+1 counters on this creature" ability does trigger. What the material I was given does NOT settle is what becomes of Blood Tyrant when Aspen leaves the game — Malevolent Whispers gave Aspen control only until end of turn and Briella remains the owner ([Malevolent Whispers ruling #0]) — nor whether the game continues (three players are named, so presumably it does, but no multiplayer or game-ending rule was provided). To resolve those pieces you'd need the rules on state-based actions, players leaving the game, and control-change effects, which weren't included here.

Timing note: I'm reading the question as Volt Charge fully resolving (damage, then proliferate) before Aspen's loss is registered, as stated. Separately, Volt Charge's proliferate could add one more +1/+1 counter to Blood Tyrant if it already had one ([Volt Charge ruling #5], [Volt Charge ruling #1]).

question: Aspen, Brycen, and Collins begin a multiplayer game. In Aspen's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Brycen. Does Aspen draw a card for the turn?
answer:

So the sequence as described is slightly off: Leyline of Anticipation is already on the battlefield when Aspen's first turn starts, and it then lets Aspen cast spells as though they had flash, which is what permits casting Desperate Ritual-style plays in an upkeep step.
- Simian Spirit Guide's exile ability and Desperate Ritual can supply the {R} mana; note [Desperate Ritual ruling #4] — Desperate Ritual is not a mana ability, so it uses the stack and can be responded to.
- Goblin Charbelcher's ability requires choosing its target as you activate it ([Goblin Charbelcher ruling #1]), so Brycen must be chosen before any cards are revealed, and Mountains double the damage.

What's missing: the rule stating that in a two-player game the starting player skips their first draw step, and whether that exception applies in a game with three players such as Aspen, Brycen, and Collins. Because the question involves more than two players and hinges precisely on that rule, I won't guess at it. question: Addison, Brixton, and Collins started playing a multiplayer game. Collins lost the game, and then Addison restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Addison draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?

What the provided material does establish:

What's missing: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules supplied to me here (they cover splice, storm, cascade, epic, copying spells, split cards, and what a spell is) address the turn structure, the draw step, or whether the starting player skips their first draw. "Starts like a game normally does" tells you the pregame procedure repeats, but it does not, on its own, tell you the draw-step rule for the first turn. What would settle it: the rule governing the first turn's draw step and how it depends on the number of players in the game (the rule usually numbered in the 103 section on starting the game).

question: Aniyah casts [Martyrdom], targeting their [Douser of Lights]. After it resolves, Nico takes control of Douser of Lights with [Act of Aggression]. Can Nico activate the ability it gained from Martyrdom?

question: Nehemiah controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ari casts [Bishop of Binding], exiling the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. When Ari attacks with Bishop of Binding on their next turn, what will X equal in Bishop of Binding's triggered ability?
answer:
X will equal 3 — and I should be explicit about my grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided in this conversation (combat/attacking rules like 506.4b, 508.7–508.7c, 702.190b, summoning sickness 302.6/602.5a, Aura rules 303.4a/303.4j, resolution rule 608.2k, priority rule 502.4, or the multiplayer range-of-influence rules 801.5a/801.7) address counters, exile, or power in non-battlefield zones. So this answer rests entirely on the card data and rulings supplied, which are themselves authoritative grounding.

Why X = 3:
- Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is neither hand nor library, so the two +1/+1 counters stay on the exiled card. This printed text overrides the general behavior stated in [Bishop of Binding ruling #1] ("Any counters on the exiled creature will cease to exist") — card text wins over a general rule it contradicts.
- [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2] confirms counters that adjust power/toughness affect Skullbriar in zones other than the battlefield, so the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a 3/3.
- Bishop of Binding's attack trigger sets X to the power of the exiled card, and [Bishop of Binding ruling #5] says that value is determined only as the ability resolves. So the target Vampire gets +3/+3 until end of turn.

Caveats: if Bishop of Binding has left the battlefield while the trigger is on the stack so no exiled card exists on resolution, X is 0 ([Bishop of Binding ruling #0]). If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave lacked its abilities in the zone it was leaving, the counters wouldn't have carried over ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]); assuming an ordinary battlefield-to-exile move, they do. Nothing here depends on player count, so the result is the same with two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Counters are not objects and have no characteristics. Notably, a counter is not a token, and a token is not a counter. Counters with the same name or description are interchangeable. A +X/+Y counter on a creature or on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield, where X and Y are numbers, adds X to that object’s power and Y to that object’s toughness. Similarly, -X/-Y counters subtract from power and toughness. See rule 613.4c.

question: Avery controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Leatherback Baloth]s with magnet counters on them. Nayeli controls one [Imperial Moth] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nayeli's legal blocks?
answer:
Honest correction: the Comprehensive Rules text provided to me in this conversation does not settle this question, so I'm setting answered to false.

What I can say from the card data alone: Magnetic Web reads "Whenever a creature with a magnet counter on it attacks, all creatures with magnet counters on them block that creature this turn if able." Since both attacking Leatherback Baloths have magnet counters, that ability triggered twice, and Nayeli's Imperial Moth (which also has a magnet counter, and which is a creature because only the face-up Imperial Moth face's characteristics are considered) is under two separate "must block" requirements — one for each Leatherback Baloth. Imperial Moth is one 2/4 creature with no ability to block more than one attacker, so it plainly cannot satisfy both.

What's missing: the provided rules include nothing about declaring blockers, blocking restrictions/requirements, or how a player resolves conflicting "blocks if able" requirements (the rules I was given cover zones, state-based actions for Auras/Equipment, players leaving multiplayer games, dies/sacrifice definitions, and look-back-in-time triggers — none of which address combat). Specifically, I have no provided rule stating that a player must choose a legal block fulfilling the maximum possible number of requirements, which is the exact principle needed to say whether Nayeli must block one Leatherback Baloth or may block neither. I won't fill that gap from memory or invent a citation.

To get a definitive answer, you'd need the declare-blockers rules (the section on blocking restrictions and requirements) added to the context.

question: Arden controls [Naga Vitalist] and a [Deathrite Shaman] that's currently a land due to [Xenograft] (naming "Saproling") and [Life and Limb]. Neither player has any land cards in their graveyards. If Arden taps Naga Vitalist, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: Naga Vitalist can be tapped for one mana of any color — {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}. Colorless {C} only if some other land Arden controls could produce it.

Important transparency point: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me are relevant here. Those excerpts cover combat triggers on declaring attackers and blockers (508.x, 509.x), triggered-ability basics (603.2f, 603.2g), multiplayer range of influence (801.7), and face-down permanents (708.3, 708.12). None of them address mana types, lands' mana abilities, or type-changing effects. So I am not citing any rule number, because doing so would be inventing support.

What does settle it is the card data and rulings supplied, which are authoritative grounding on their own:
- Xenograft: each creature Arden controls is the chosen type (Saproling) in addition to its other types, so Deathrite Shaman is a Saproling.
- Life and Limb: all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types; Life and Limb ruling #3 confirms it has both the creature and land card types with subtypes Forest and Saproling, and Life and Limb ruling #2 gives each Forest "{T}: Add {G}".
- So Deathrite Shaman is a land Arden controls whose mana-producing effects include "Add {G}" and its own "{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color."
- Naga Vitalist ruling #0: Naga Vitalist checks the effects of lands' mana-producing abilities but not their costs or legality — so the empty graveyards and the unsatisfiable target don't matter. Naga Vitalist ruling #3: restrictions and riders are ignored. Naga Vitalist ruling #1: gained land types/abilities can change what a land can produce. Naga Vitalist ruling #2: the types of mana are the five colors plus colorless.

Caveat: Deathrite Shaman ruling #1 notes that its first ability targets and so is not a mana ability. It is still a land ability whose effect adds mana, which is why the any-color result holds; if your group reads "could produce" as limited to true mana abilities, Naga Vitalist would only make {G}.

Nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.106.7: Some abilities produce mana based on the type of mana another permanent or permanents “could produce.” The type of mana a permanent could produce at any time includes any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time, taking into account any applicable replacement effects in any possible order. Ignore whether any costs of the ability could or could not be paid. If that permanent wouldn’t produce any mana under these conditions, or no type of mana can be defined this way, there’s no type of mana it could produce. Exotic Orchard has the ability “{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce.” If your opponent controls no lands, activating Exotic Orchard’s mana ability will produce no mana. The same is true if you and your opponent each control no lands other than Exotic Orchards. However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.
gold_text.608.2b: If the object that’s resolving is an instant spell, a sorcery spell, or an ability, its resolution may involve several steps. The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last. If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal. A target that’s no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted is illegal. Other changes to the game state may cause a target to no longer be legal; for example, its characteristics may have changed or an effect may have changed the text of the spell. If the source of an ability has left the zone it was in, its last known information is used during this process. If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve. It’s removed from the stack and, if it’s a spell, put into its owner’s graveyard. Otherwise, the spell or ability will resolve normally. Illegal targets, if any, won’t be affected by parts of a resolving spell’s effect for which they’re illegal. Other parts of the effect for which those targets are not illegal may still affect them. If the spell or ability creates any continuous effects that affect game rules (see rule 613.11), those effects don’t apply to illegal targets. If part of the effect requires information about an illegal target, it fails to determine any such information. Any part of the effect that requires that information won’t happen. Sorin’s Thirst is a black instant that reads, “Sorin’s Thirst deals 2 damage to target creature and you gain 2 life.” If the creature isn’t a legal target during the resolution of Sorin’s Thirst (say, if the creature has gained protection from black or left the battlefield), then Sorin’s Thirst doesn’t resolve. Its controller doesn’t gain any life. Plague Spores reads, “Destroy target nonblack creature and target land. They can’t be regenerated.” Suppose the same creature land is chosen both as the nonblack creature and as the land, and the color of the creature land is changed to black before Plague Spores resolves. Plague Spores still resolves because the black creature land is still a legal target for the “target land” part of the spell. The “destroy target nonblack creature” part of the spell won’t affect that permanent, but the “destroy target land” part of the spell will still destroy it. It can’t be regenerated.

answer_gold: Any color. Naga Vitalist checks to see what mana Deathrite Shaman could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. If Deathrite Shaman's first ability were to resolve now it would produce any color of mana. It doesn't matter that it has no legal targets and couldn't resolve, since the check in [106.7] takes it resolving as a premise.

question: Adelyn controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Dwarven Trader] and [Staunch Shieldmate] in their graveyard. They cast [Animate Dead] targeting Dwarven Trader. What happens as it enters the battlefield?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged): Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield ability triggers twice — once normally and once more from Panharmonicon, because Mycosynth Lattice makes Animate Dead an artifact permanent — and only the first instance does anything: Dwarven Trader returns to the battlefield under Adelyn's control with Animate Dead attached. The second instance resolves but returns nothing; Staunch Shieldmate stays in the graveyard.

Important honesty note about grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (707.4, 707.9g, 707.10e, 610.3b, 616.1f, 722.3c, 701.15d, and the various "multiple instances of [keyword] trigger separately" rules) do not address Panharmonicon-style extra triggers or Animate Dead's reanimation. This answer rests on the card texts and the provided card rulings, which are authoritative on their own, plus the provided glossary entry for the intervening "if" clause. The only numbered rule I lean on is 707.10e, which defines copying a spell or ability as putting a copy of it onto the stack — that is not what Panharmonicon does (per Panharmonicon ruling #8, it causes the ability to trigger an additional time, with modes, targets, and resolution choices made separately for each instance).

Step by step:

1. Mycosynth Lattice: "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types." Once Animate Dead is on the battlefield it is an artifact Aura. It was not an artifact while it was a spell on the stack (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1).
2. Panharmonicon: "If an artifact or creature entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time." This applies to a permanent's own enters-the-battlefield trigger (Panharmonicon ruling #4) and to abilities triggered by a permanent entering at the same time as, or including, itself (Panharmonicon ruling #1). So Animate Dead's "When this Aura enters" ability triggers twice.
3. First instance: the intervening "if" clause ("if it's on the battlefield") is checked both when the ability would trigger and again as it resolves. Animate Dead is on the battlefield, so it resolves: Animate Dead loses "enchant creature card in a graveyard," gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returns Dwarven Trader to the battlefield under Adelyn's control, and attaches to it (Animate Dead ruling #1).
4. Second instance: the "if" condition is still met, so it resolves, but there is no enchanted creature card in a graveyard to return — Animate Dead is now attached to Dwarven Trader on the battlefield and cannot be moved to anything else (Animate Dead ruling #3). So nothing happens, and Staunch Shieldmate is not reanimated.
5. End state: Dwarven Trader is a colorless artifact creature — Dwarf (Mycosynth Lattice rulings #1 and #2) and is 0/1 because Animate Dead gives enchanted creature -1/-0.

Timing assumption: I assume both Panharmonicon and Mycosynth Lattice were already on the battlefield when Animate Dead entered. If Mycosynth Lattice were not in play, Animate Dead would be a non-artifact enchantment, Panharmonicon would not double its trigger, and you'd get a single trigger — same end result of Dwarven Trader returning.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players; the outcome is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.611.3c: A continuous effect may be generated by the static ability of an object. Continuous effects that modify characteristics of permanents do so simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield. They don’t wait until the permanent is on the battlefield and then change it. Because such effects apply as the permanent enters the battlefield, they are applied before determining whether the permanent will cause an ability to trigger when it enters the battlefield. A permanent with the static ability “All white creatures get +1/+1” is on the battlefield. A creature spell that would normally create a 1/1 white creature instead creates a 2/2 white creature. The creature doesn’t enter the battlefield as 1/1 and then change to 2/2.

cited_text.707.10e: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. Some effects copy a spell or ability and specify a new target for the copy. If the spell or ability has more than one target, each of the copy’s targets must be that player or object. If that player or object isn’t a legal target for each instance of the word “target,” the copy isn’t created. In the case where a replacement effect causes the copy to target more than one object, the copy’s controller chooses one of them to be the new target. The chosen target must be a legal target for that spell or ability. Frontline Heroism is an enchantment with the ability “Whenever you cast a spell that targets only a single creature you control, create a 1/1 red Soldier creature token with haste, then copy that spell. The copy targets that token.” Anointed Procession is an enchantment with the ability “If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead.” If you control both and cast Moment of Triumph targeting a creature you control, Frontline Heroism’s ability triggers. As that ability resolves, you create two 1/1 red Soldier creature tokens with haste, then copy Moment of Triumph and the copy targets one of those tokens of your choice. The copy doesn’t target both the tokens.
cited_text.Intervening “If” Clause: Intervening “If” Clause. A specially worded condition checked as a triggered ability would trigger and again as it would resolve. See rule 603.4.

answer_gold: Animate Dead enters the battlefield attached to Dwarven Trader and triggers twice. The first trigger will return Dwarven Trader to the battlefield. The second trigger just does the same things again, so it has no relevant result.

question: Armani controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Canopy Vista]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Canopy Vista. Can Armani attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
Yes — Armani can declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico. To be transparent: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (603.10a, 608.2b, 616.1f, 700.3a, 702.80b/d, 702.153b, 712.21d, 724.1b/c, 724.2b/c, 801.7a, 120.4c) address declaring attackers, attack restrictions, or characteristic-defining power/toughness. My answer therefore rests entirely on the card text and rulings supplied, which are authoritative on this interaction.

Reverence reads "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you," so power is checked as attackers are declared. [Gaea's Liege ruling #0] states directly: "When being declared as an attacker, use the 'not attacking' power and toughness. It only changes after declaration is complete." Gaea's Liege's not-attacking power equals the number of Forests Armani controls. Armani's 3 Canopy Vistas have the Forest land type — [Canopy Vista ruling #0] confirms these lands really do have the basic land type Forest, and [Canopy Vista ruling #1] notes they still aren't basic lands. So Gaea's Liege is 3/3 at declaration; 3 is not "2 or less," and Reverence does not stop the attack.

After declaration completes, Gaea's Liege becomes equal to the number of Forests Nico (the defending player) controls — 1 Canopy Vista — so it attacks as a 1/1. Nothing in the supplied material re-checks Reverence after attackers are legally declared. Note also that tapping Gaea's Liege for its {T} ability would prevent it from attacking that turn, and per [Reverence ruling #0] a creature that can't attack Nico could still attack a planeswalker Nico controls.

Multiplayer note: the provided material doesn't include multiplayer attack rules, but Reverence only protects Nico; against a different opponent Gaea's Liege's attacking power would count that defending player's Forests instead.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.508.1c: First, the active player declares attackers. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. To declare attackers, the active player follows the steps below, in order. If at any point during the declaration of attackers, the active player is unable to comply with any of the steps listed below, the declaration is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the declaration (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). The active player checks each creature they control to see whether it’s affected by any restrictions (effects that say a creature can’t attack, or that it can’t attack unless some condition is met). If any restrictions are being disobeyed, the declaration of attackers is illegal. A player controls two creatures, each with a restriction that states “This creature can’t attack alone.” It’s legal to declare both as attackers.
gold_text.508.1j: First, the active player declares attackers. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. To declare attackers, the active player follows the steps below, in order. If at any point during the declaration of attackers, the active player is unable to comply with any of the steps listed below, the declaration is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the declaration (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). Once the player has enough mana in their mana pool, they pay all costs in any order. Partial payments are not allowed.

answer_gold: Yes. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".

question: Ariel attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Charnel Serenade]?
answer:
Honest correction: the Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not settle this question. The numbered rules provided here cover X placeholders (107.1c, 107.3, 107.3j, 107.3m), ward, bloodthirst, monstrosity, blight, graft, counters (122.1a), loyalty (306.5c), star power/toughness (208.2a), class level bars (716.2d), and the Walker token — none of them address suspend, special actions, or what "cast without paying its mana cost" permits. So I can't ground the answer in the provided rules text.

What I can say rests on the card rulings supplied, which are authoritative on their own: Ariel cannot suspend Charnel Serenade off Wildfire Eternal's trigger. Exiling a card with suspend isn't casting it and doesn't use the stack [Charnel Serenade ruling #15], while Wildfire Eternal's trigger only grants permission to cast an instant or sorcery from hand without paying its mana cost. Additionally, casting a card without paying its mana cost doesn't let you pay alternative costs [Charnel Serenade ruling #4], [Wildfire Eternal ruling #6], and suspend may only be used when Ariel could actually cast the card [Charnel Serenade ruling #10] — Charnel Serenade is a sorcery, so not during the declare blockers step.

Ariel can instead cast Charnel Serenade itself for free at that moment; the trigger ignores the normal sorcery timing, and it must be done as the trigger resolves [Wildfire Eternal ruling #0]. I'm assuming the trigger arose in the declare blockers step with no blockers declared [Wildfire Eternal ruling #4]. Nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table on the basis of the rules I was given.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.62a: Suspend Suspend is a keyword that represents three abilities. The first is a static ability that functions while the card with suspend is in a player’s hand. The second and third are triggered abilities that function in the exile zone. “Suspend N—[cost]” means “If you could begin to cast this card by putting it onto the stack from your hand, you may pay [cost] and exile it with N time counters on it. This action doesn’t use the stack,” and “At the beginning of your upkeep, if this card is suspended, remove a time counter from it,” and “When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it’s exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don’t, it remains exiled. If you cast a creature spell this way, it gains haste until you lose control of the spell or the permanent it becomes.”

answer_gold:
Yes. The suspend special action can be taken whenever Charnel Serenade could be cast from Ariel's hand. Normally that's only when Ariel has priority on their turn with an empty stack, but in this case the effect of Wildfire Eternal is letting that happen while the ability resolves.

(They still have to pay the suspend cost, and afterwards they can choose to cast a different spell from hand without paying its mana cost.)

question: Brynn has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Fairgrounds Warden] that exiled Coleman's [Alpha Tyrranax]. Aspen casts [Psychic Purge], targeting Brynn. What happens as Brynn loses the game?
answer:
Alpha Tyrranax returns to the battlefield under Coleman's control. Psychic Purge deals 1 damage to Brynn, dropping Brynn to 0 life, and Brynn loses the game and leaves it. All objects Brynn owned leave the game, so the phased-out Fairgrounds Warden leaves the battlefield — and the moment it does, the one-shot effect that exiled Alpha Tyrranax returns that card to the battlefield.

Details:

- Being phased out doesn't protect Fairgrounds Warden or delay anything. A phased-out permanent is still on the battlefield; when Brynn leaves the game it stops existing, which counts as Fairgrounds Warden leaving the battlefield. ("Phased out" simply means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist for most purposes.)
- The return isn't a triggered ability, so rule 800.4d — which says a triggered ability controlled by a player who has left the game is never put onto the stack — doesn't stop it. This is exactly the case covered by [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #0]: if Fairgrounds Warden's owner leaves the game, the exiled card still returns.
- The return happens immediately after Fairgrounds Warden leaves the battlefield, with nothing in between, not even state-based actions [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #2].
- Alpha Tyrranax comes back under its owner Coleman's control, not Brynn's or Aspen's, per rule 610.3c.
- If Alpha Tyrranax had been a token rather than a card, it would have ceased to exist and would not return [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #1].

This answer assumes the multiplayer setting the question describes (at least Brynn, Coleman, and Aspen), where the game continues after Brynn leaves (rule 800.4d). In a two-player game, the game would simply end when Brynn lost, so the return would be irrelevant.

Psychic Purge's second ability doesn't apply here — that only triggers when an opponent's spell or ability makes Brynn discard Psychic Purge, which isn't what happened.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.26b: Phasing If a permanent phases out, its status changes to “phased out.” Except for rules and effects that specifically mention phased-out permanents, a phased-out permanent is treated as though it does not exist. It can’t affect or be affected by anything else in the game. A permanent that phases out is removed from combat. (See rule 506.4.) You control three creatures, one of which is phased out. You cast a spell that says “Draw a card for each creature you control.” You draw two cards. You control a phased-out creature. You cast a spell that says “Destroy all creatures.” The phased-out creature is not destroyed.
gold_text.702.26k: Phasing Phased-out permanents owned by a player who leaves the game also leave the game. This doesn’t cause zone-change abilities to trigger. See rule 800.4.
gold_text.800.4a: Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game. When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end. Then, if that player controlled any objects on the stack not represented by cards, those objects cease to exist. Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game. If the player who left the game had priority at the time they left, priority passes to the next player in turn order who’s still in the game. Alex casts Mind Control, an Aura that reads, “You control enchanted creature,” on Bianca’s Assault Griffin. If Alex leaves the game, so does Mind Control, and Assault Griffin reverts to Bianca’s control. If, instead, Bianca leaves the game, so does Assault Griffin, and Mind Control is put into Alex’s graveyard. Alex casts Act of Treason, which reads, in part, “Gain control of target creature until end of turn,” targeting Bianca’s Runeclaw Bears. If Alex leaves the game, Act of Treason’s change-of-control effect ends and Runeclaw Bears reverts to Bianca’s control. Alex casts Bribery, which reads, “Search target opponent’s library for a creature card and put that card onto the battlefield under your control. Then that player shuffles their library,” targeting Bianca. Alex puts Serra Angel onto the battlefield from Bianca’s library. If Bianca leaves the game, Serra Angel also leaves the game. If, instead, Alex leaves the game, Serra Angel is exiled. Alex controls Genesis Chamber, which reads, “Whenever a nontoken creature enters, if Genesis Chamber is untapped, that creature’s controller creates a 1/1 colorless Myr artifact creature token.” If Alex leaves the game, all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under Alex’s control leave the game, and all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under any other player’s control remain in the game.

cited_text.610.3c: Some one-shot effects cause an object to change zones “until” a specified event occurs. A second one-shot effect is created immediately after the specified event. This second one-shot effect returns the object to its previous zone. An object returned to the battlefield this way returns under its owner’s control unless otherwise specified.
cited_text.800.4d: Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game. If an object that would be owned by a player who has left the game would be created in any zone, it isn’t created. If a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game would be put onto the stack, it isn’t put on the stack. Astral Slide is an enchantment that reads, “Whenever a player cycles a card, you may exile target creature. If you do, return that creature to the battlefield under its owner’s control at the beginning of the next end step.” During Alex’s turn, Bianca uses Astral Slide’s ability to exile Alex’s Hypnotic Specter. Before the end of that turn, Bianca leaves the game. At the beginning of the end step, the delayed triggered ability generated by Astral Slide that would return Hypnotic Specter to the battlefield triggers, but it isn’t put on the stack. Hypnotic Specter never returns to the battlefield.

answer_gold: All objects owned by Brynn leave the game. However the game treats phased-out permanents as nonexistent, and does not see the leaves-the-battlefield event happen. Alpha Tyrranax will not return to the battlefield.

question: Avery controls [Caelorna, Coral Tyrant] and [Darksteel Garrison] that's fortifying [Spire Garden]. Avery casts [Bludgeon Brawl]. After that resolves they activate Darksteel Garrison's equip ability targeting Caelorna, Coral Tyrant. What does the battlefield look like after that ability has resolved and state-based actions have been checked?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules text I was given does not settle this question. Setting answered to false for that reason.

The numbered rules provided here cover unrelated ground — replacement-effect ordering and choices (400.6, 616.1e, 616.1f, 608.2c), melded and merged permanents leaving the battlefield (712.21c, 712.21d, 712.5d, 730.3c, 730.3d), look-back-in-time triggers (603.10a), destruction/regeneration (701.8c), damage processing (120.4c), phasing (702.26h), and multiple instances of annihilator/modular (702.86b, 702.43b). None of them address Equipment, Fortifications, equip abilities, attaching or unattaching permanents, or the state-based actions that check whether an attachment is legal — which is exactly what this question turns on.

What I can say from the card data provided (rulings, which are ground truth, but not Comprehensive Rules): Bludgeon Brawl makes Darksteel Garrison — a noncreature, non-Equipment artifact with mana value 2 — an Equipment with equip {2} and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0," and Darksteel Garrison keeps its other types and abilities [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #0], so it is still a Fortification. Fortifications otherwise follow the same rules as Equipment [Darksteel Garrison ruling #2], and a dual-type attachment made into an Equipment can be moved with its granted equip ability [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #1]. That points to Darksteel Garrison ending up attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant (0/8 base, so 2/8 while equipped), no longer fortifying Spire Garden, which therefore loses indestructible and its becomes-tapped trigger. If Bludgeon Brawl later leaves the battlefield or Darksteel Garrison becomes a creature, Darksteel Garrison stops being an Equipment and becomes unattached while staying on the battlefield [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2].

To confirm the attachment-legality state-based action and the exact behavior of a permanent that is both Fortification and Equipment, I'd need the Comprehensive Rules sections on Equipment/Fortifications and on state-based actions for illegal attachments, which were not provided.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.205.1a: The type line is printed directly below the illustration. It contains the card’s card type(s). It also contains the card’s subtype(s) and supertype(s), if applicable. Some effects set an object’s card type. In most such cases, the new card type(s) replaces any existing card types. However, an object with either the instant or sorcery card type retains that type. Counters, stickers, effects, and damage marked on the object remain with it, even if they are meaningless to the new card type. Similarly, when an effect sets one or more of an object’s subtypes, the new subtype(s) replaces any existing subtypes from the appropriate set (creature types, land types, artifact types, enchantment types, planeswalker types, or spell types). If an object’s card type is removed, the subtypes correlated with that card type will remain if they are also the subtypes of a card type the object currently has; otherwise, they are also removed for the entire time the object’s card type is removed. Removing an object’s subtype doesn’t affect its card types at all.
gold_text.301.5: Some artifacts have the subtype “Equipment.” An Equipment can be attached to a creature. It can’t legally be attached to anything that isn’t a creature.
gold_text.301.5c: Some artifacts have the subtype “Equipment.” An Equipment can be attached to a creature. It can’t legally be attached to anything that isn’t a creature. An Equipment that’s also a creature can’t equip a creature unless that Equipment has reconfigure (see rule 702.151, “Reconfigure”). An Equipment that loses the subtype “Equipment” can’t equip a creature. An Equipment can’t equip itself. An Equipment that equips an illegal or nonexistent permanent becomes unattached from that permanent but remains on the battlefield. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.) An Equipment can’t equip more than one creature. If a spell or ability would cause an Equipment to equip more than one creature, the Equipment’s controller chooses which creature it equips.

answer_gold:
Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant and not to Spire Garden.

Bludgeon Brawl doesn't specify that the permanents it affects keep their original subtypes, so they are overwritten. This means that Darksteel Garrison ceases to be a Fortification as soon as Bludgeon Brawl enters the battlefield. It will become unattached the next time state-based actions are performed. When its equip ability resolves, it becomes attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can target Pristine Angel with Murder even though Pristine Angel is now untapped.

Why: Pristine Angel's own text grants protection from artifacts and from each color only "as long as this creature is untapped." While Pristine Angel was tapped and attacking, it had no protection at all, so Cephalid Snitch's ability ("Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn") legally targeted it. That ability creates a continuous effect lasting until end of turn: for the rest of this turn, Pristine Angel does not have protection from black. When Abel casts a spell and uses Pristine Angel's triggered ability to untap it, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from every color except black, because Cephalid Snitch's until-end-of-turn effect is still shutting off protection from black. Murder is a black spell, so it can target and destroy Pristine Angel (Pristine Angel is a 4/4 with no other protective ability).

Timing note: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved while Pristine Angel was untapped-less (i.e., tapped), as stated. If instead Nico tried to activate Cephalid Snitch's ability targeting Pristine Angel while Pristine Angel was untapped, the targeting would be illegal in the first place (protection from black stops it being targeted by a black source), and Murder would likewise be unable to target it.

Side note: Nico casting Murder targeting a permanent Abel controls commits a crime, which matters only if some card cares about crimes [700.13].

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.7a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. A continuous effect generated by a static ability has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later. If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same. Rune of Flight is an Aura that grants enchanted Equipment “Equipped creature has flying.” A player attaches Rune of Flight to Colossus Hammer, an Equipment with “Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying.” The ability granted by Rune of Flight shares Rune of Flight’s timestamp because it is later than Colossus Hammer’s timestamp. If Colossus Hammer becomes attached to a creature, both of its abilities receive new timestamps (see rule 613.7e), but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same.
gold_text.702.16h: Protection “Protection from each [characteristic]” is shorthand for “protection from [quality A],” “protection from [quality B],” and so on for each possible quality the listed characteristic could have; it behaves as multiple separate protection abilities.

cited_text.700.13: Some cards refer to committing a crime. A player commits a crime as that player casts a spell, activates an ability, or puts a triggered ability on the stack and that spell or ability targets at least one opponent; at least one permanent, spell, or ability an opponent controls; and/or at least one card in an opponent’s graveyard.

answer_gold:
Yes. "Protection from all colors" is shorthand for protection from each color individually. It loses protection from black, and still has protection from all the other colors.

(The timestamp of Pristine Angel's ability does not change when it becomes untapped.)

question: Adelyn controls [Back from the Brink] and has [Shifting Wall] in their graveyard. Can Adelyn activate Back from the Brink's ability to create a token of Shifting Wall? Can they pay more than {0} to do so? If so, will it enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Yes, Adelyn can activate Back from the Brink's ability exiling Shifting Wall, but the cost paid is effectively {0}, no more, and the token enters with no +1/+1 counters.

Back from the Brink's ability requires exiling a creature card from your graveyard and paying its mana cost. Shifting Wall's mana cost is just {X}. Per [Back from the Brink ruling #3], if the exiled creature card has {X} in its mana cost, X is considered to be zero — Adelyn doesn't get to choose a larger value, so the total paid is {0} and there is no way to pay more.

Shifting Wall's own text says "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it." That "enters with" ability does apply to the token ([Back from the Brink ruling #2] confirms "as [this creature] enters" and "[this creature] enters with" abilities work), but with X = 0 it enters with zero +1/+1 counters. Since Shifting Wall's printed power/toughness is 0/0, the token is a 0/0 creature and will be put into the graveyard as a state-based action for having 0 toughness essentially immediately.

Note also that the token copy has defender, which means it can't attack ([702.3b]), so it would only ever be useful as a blocker — and at 0/0 with no counters it won't survive to block anyway. Nothing here depends on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.107.3h: Many objects use the letter X as a placeholder for a number that needs to be determined. Some objects have abilities that define the value of X; the rest let their controller choose the value of X. If an effect instructs a player to pay an object’s mana cost that includes {X}, the value of X is treated as 0 unless the object is a spell on the stack. In that case, the value of X is the value chosen or determined for it as the spell was cast.

cited_text.702.3b: Defender A creature with defender can’t attack.

answer_gold: Adelyn may activate the ability of Shifting Wall paying {0}. He does not have the ability to pay more than {0}. The token will not enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters.

question: Alex controls a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], a [Mycosynth Lattice], and a [Control Magic] that took control of a [Boris Devilboon] from Nico. Alex begins activating the ability of Boris Devilboon and sacrifices Control Magic to help pay the cost. Is this legal? If so, who will control the ability?
answer:
Yes, it's legal, and Alex controls the ability (and gets the Minor Demon token).

Why sacrificing Control Magic works: Mycosynth Lattice says "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types," and that explicitly includes Auras — the ruling confirms "The Lattice's first ability causes Auras to become artifacts" [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3]. So Control Magic, an Aura on the battlefield, is an artifact and is a legal thing to sacrifice to Krark-Clan Ironworks' cost "Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}." Note the mana produced is {C}{C} (colorless specifically), but Boris Devilboon's cost is {2}{B}{R}, {T} — the {2} is generic, so the two {C} pay that part; the {B} and {R} must still come from elsewhere, though Mycosynth Lattice's third ability ("Players may spend mana as though it were mana of any color") lets Alex spend colorless mana as though it were black or red, so the {C}{C} could instead pay {B}{R} if Alex has other mana for the generic {2}.

Why Alex keeps the ability: Alex controlled Boris Devilboon at the moment the ability was activated (Control Magic: "You control enchanted creature"), so Alex is the ability's controller, and the ability exists independently on the stack once activated. Sacrificing Control Magic during the payment of costs means Boris Devilboon immediately reverts to Nico's control (tapped, since {T} was paid), but that does not change who controls the already-activated ability or undo it. The token is created under Alex's control.

Timing note: I'm assuming Alex activates the ability first and sacrifices Control Magic while paying costs (as stated). If instead Control Magic were sacrificed before activation, Alex would no longer control Boris Devilboon and could not activate its ability at all.

Multiplayer: nothing changes with more than two players here — the only provided multiplayer rule concerns a player leaving the game, in which case an ability that would be controlled by a departed player isn't put on the stack [800.4d]; that doesn't apply while Alex is still in the game.

question: Nico has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Aiden controls a [Chronatog Totem] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts an [Evil Twin], choosing to have it copy Chronatog Totem. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged in substance, but now stated with its actual grounding): Evil Twin enters the battlefield under Nico's control, and Nico — not Aiden — makes the copy choice.

Important caveat about sourcing: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (about blight, amass, scavenge, embalm, graft, shuffling, layers, and state-based actions) do not address Gather Specimens, control-changing entry replacements, or copy effects. So this answer rests entirely on the card rulings provided as ground truth, not on the numbered rules text; if you want a rules-number citation, the relevant CR sections weren't supplied here.

From the provided card rulings:
- Gather Specimens isn't targeted and affects creatures that would enter under any opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #4], and it applies to creatures entering by any means, including resolving creature spells [Gather Specimens ruling #7]. Evil Twin is such a spell, so the permanent enters under Nico's control; casting choices are remembered and "enters" triggers happen after it's under Nico's control [Gather Specimens ruling #6].
- Gather Specimens' replacement effect is applied before other effects that modify how the creature enters, and the explicit example is that if Clone would enter under an opponent's control, you choose which creature it copies as it enters under your control [Gather Specimens ruling #3]. Evil Twin's "you may have this creature enter as a copy" is that same kind of effect, so Aiden's intent to copy Chronatog Totem is not binding — Nico chooses, and may choose nothing, in which case Evil Twin is a 0/0 and goes to the graveyard [Evil Twin ruling #4].
- If Nico does copy Chronatog Totem, only Chronatog Totem's printed copiable values are copied, not the non-copy effect that made it a creature until end of turn [Evil Twin ruling #7]. So it enters as a noncreature artifact named Chronatog Totem with its three abilities plus "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature" — it has no power/toughness and doesn't die. Even if Nico pays {1}{U} to animate it, it can't attack or use "{T}: Add {U}" this turn, because its controller must have controlled the permanent continuously since the beginning of their most recent turn [Chronatog Totem ruling #0].

Timing: I'm assuming Gather Specimens resolved before Evil Twin was cast, as stated; it doesn't retroactively change control of creatures that already entered [Gather Specimens ruling #0]. Had Gather Specimens come after Evil Twin entered, Evil Twin would stay under Aiden's control with Aiden's copy choice.

Multiplayer: same result with more than two players, since Gather Specimens hits creatures entering under any opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #4]; if multiple Gather Specimens were cast this turn, the would-be controller chooses which applies first and the process repeats [Gather Specimens ruling #5], which can leave the creature with its original controller when two opposing players each cast one [Gather Specimens ruling #8].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

question: Albert and Nico are beginning the game and have just drawn 7 cards. Albert has [Serum Powder] in their hand. Does Albert get to know whether Nico is going to mulligan before deciding whether to use Serum Powder's ability?
answer:
The provided rules don't settle this. Nothing in the context includes the mulligan procedure (rule 103.4 and its steps), which is what governs the order in which players decide to mulligan and how much information each player has before deciding. Serum Powder's own text only tells us when Albert may use the ability — "Any time you could mulligan and this card is in your hand" — and its rulings only confirm that using it doesn't prevent further mulligans and that the exiled cards stay exiled for the game [Serum Powder ruling #0] [Serum Powder ruling #1].

The closest general principle in the context is the APNAP rule: when multiple players would make choices at the same time, the active player chooses first, then each other player in turn order, and a later player knows the choices already made [101.4b]. That would suggest whichever of Albert or Nico chooses second knows the earlier player's decision, but the mulligan step is not framed as a simultaneous-choice event by any rule given here, so applying [101.4b] to it would be a guess. Note also that the question involves two players (Albert and Nico); with more than two players the turn-order sequencing of such choices could matter more, but again the mulligan rules needed to say so aren't provided.

What's missing: the mulligan procedure rules (order of mulligan declarations and whether they're simultaneous or sequential).

Once each player has made a declaration, all players who decided to take mulligans do so at the same time. To take a mulligan, a player shuffles the cards in their hand back into their library, draws a new hand of cards equal to their starting hand size, then puts a number of those cards equal to the number of times that player has taken a mulligan on the bottom of their library in any order. question: Ariana controls [Sen Triplets], which targeted Nico. Nico's hand contains [Rift Sower]. Can either player suspend it? If so, who will cast it once the last time counter is removed?
answer:
Direct answer: Neither player can suspend Rift Sower this turn. Ariana may simply cast Rift Sower from Nico's hand for {2}{G} instead.

Important note on grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me in this conversation are all about mana production and related topics (106.5, 106.6, 106.6a, 106.7, 106.9, 106.10, 106.11, 106.12a, 106.12b, 607.5a, 609.4b, 613.1a, 701.10f). None of them address suspend, special actions, or casting spells from another player's hand, so I cannot cite a numbered rule for this answer. My answer rests entirely on the card text and the card rulings supplied above, which are authoritative on their own:

- Suspending is not casting: "Exiling a card with suspend isn't casting that card" [Rift Sower ruling #4], and suspend's first ability is a static ability that lets you exile the card from hand by paying its suspend cost — {G} with two time counters for Rift Sower [Rift Sower ruling #8].
- Ariana can't suspend it: Sen Triplets' text grants only "You may play lands and cast spells from that player's hand this turn," and it "doesn't allow you to play more than one land during your turn or change when you may cast spells from the target opponent's hand" [Sen Triplets ruling #4]. That permission covers casting, not the special action of exiling a card from Nico's hand with suspend.
- Nico can't suspend it: you may exile a card with suspend only at a time when you could cast that card, accounting for effects that stop you from casting it [Rift Sower ruling #0]. Sen Triplets says Nico "can't cast spells or activate abilities" this turn, so there is no such time. Sen Triplets also shuts off all of Nico's activated abilities including mana abilities [Sen Triplets ruling #5], so Nico couldn't even produce the {G}.
- Who would cast it later: the second and third suspend abilities are triggered abilities of the exiled card, and the third gives its controller the option to cast the card when the last time counter is removed [Rift Sower ruling #8], [Rift Sower ruling #5]. Sen Triplets reaches only cards in Nico's hand, so if Nico had suspended Rift Sower on an earlier turn, Nico — not Ariana — would be the one offered the chance to cast it. Triggered abilities aren't stopped by Sen Triplets [Sen Triplets ruling #3], but if the last counter came off while Nico was the named opponent, Nico couldn't actually cast it, and the card would stay in exile with no time counters and no longer be suspended [Rift Sower ruling #5].

Timing assumption: I assume Sen Triplets' upkeep trigger has already resolved naming Nico. If instead we're looking at a moment before that trigger resolved, Nico could suspend Rift Sower normally.

Player count: Sen Triplets targets one opponent, so in a game with more than two players only Nico is restricted; other opponents could suspend their own cards freely. The Ariana/Nico analysis is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.62a: Suspend Suspend is a keyword that represents three abilities. The first is a static ability that functions while the card with suspend is in a player’s hand. The second and third are triggered abilities that function in the exile zone. “Suspend N—[cost]” means “If you could begin to cast this card by putting it onto the stack from your hand, you may pay [cost] and exile it with N time counters on it. This action doesn’t use the stack,” and “At the beginning of your upkeep, if this card is suspended, remove a time counter from it,” and “When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it’s exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don’t, it remains exiled. If you cast a creature spell this way, it gains haste until you lose control of the spell or the permanent it becomes.”

answer_gold: Neither player can suspend it. Only a card's owner has the option to suspend it, and only if they have permission to cast it.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Honest answer: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given don't settle this question. The rules provided cover suspend (116.2f, 702.62a–d), special actions (116.2e, 405.6d), split second (702.61b), beginning to cast spells (601.3b), triggered abilities (603.2a, 603.3d), ending the combat phase (724.2f), firebending (702.189a–b), and airbend (701.65b). None of them address manifest, turning a permanent face up, or the layer system that decides how Turn to Frog's ability-removing and characteristic-setting effect interacts with a permanent whose copiable characteristics change afterward — which is exactly what this question hinges on.

What the provided card data does support, without the layer rules:
- Turn to Frog reads "Until end of turn, target creature loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1," so its effect lasts until end of turn rather than ending when something about the permanent changes.
- Turn to Frog ruling #1: the affected creature loses its other colors and creature types but keeps other card types and supertypes.
- Turn to Frog ruling #3: if the creature gains an ability after Turn to Frog resolves, it keeps that ability.
- Wayward Angel's Threshold text is what would make it black, +3/+3, trample, and give the upkeep sacrifice trigger; Wayward Angel ruling #0 confirms it would be black, not white and black.

The unresolved piece is whether turning Wayward Angel face up counts as "gaining" its printed abilities after Turn to Frog resolved (ruling #3) or is instead a change to copiable characteristics that Turn to Frog keeps overwriting. Answering that requires the layer/timestamp rules and the manifest rules, and neither was provided to me. To resolve it at a table, you'd need CR 613 (interaction of continuous effects) and CR 701.34/711 (manifest and face-down permanents).

Nothing in the provided material suggests the answer differs between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.1e: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 5: Color-changing effects are applied.
gold_text.613.1f: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 6: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that say an object can’t have an ability are applied.
gold_text.613.3: Within layers 2–6, apply effects from characteristic-defining abilities first (see rule 604.3), then all other effects in timestamp order (see rule 613.7). Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a layer. (See rule 613.8.)
gold_text.613.6: If an effect should be applied in different layers and/or sublayers, the parts of the effect each apply in their appropriate ones. If an effect starts to apply in one layer and/or sublayer, it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer and/or sublayer, even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process. An effect that reads “This creature gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice until end of turn” is both a power- and toughness-changing effect and a color-changing effect. The “becomes the color of your choice” part is applied in layer 5, and then the “gets +1/+1” part is applied in layer 7c. Act of Treason has an effect that reads “Gain control of target creature until end of turn. Untap that creature. It gains haste until end of turn.” This is both a control-changing effect and an effect that adds an ability to an object. The “gain control” part is applied in layer 2, and then the “it gains haste” part is applied in layer 6. An effect that reads “All noncreature artifacts become 2/2 artifact creatures until end of turn” is both a type-changing effect and a power- and toughness-setting effect. The type-changing effect is applied to all noncreature artifacts in layer 4 and the power- and toughness-setting effect is applied to those same permanents in layer 7b, even though those permanents aren’t noncreature artifacts by then. Svogthos, the Restless Tomb, is on the battlefield. An effect that says “Until end of turn, target land becomes a 3/3 creature that’s still a land” is applied to it (layers 4 and 7b). An effect that says “Target creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn” is applied to it (layer 7c), making it a 4/4 land creature. Then while you have ten creature cards in your graveyard, you activate Svogthos’s ability: “Until end of turn, this land becomes a black and green Plant Zombie creature with ‘This creature’s power and toughness are each equal to the number of creature cards in your graveyard.’ It’s still a land.” (layers 4, 5, and 7b). It becomes an 11/11 land creature. If a creature card enters or leaves your graveyard, Svogthos’s power and toughness will be modified accordingly. If the first effect is applied to it again, it will become a 4/4 land creature again.
